en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Nantang Lia’an When I was in my prime, I formed a spiritual friendship with Master Qianyan Chang. Master Qianyan showed me a verse and eulogy by Chan Master Nantang;
upon reading it, I was struck with awe and said, "These are the words of one who has attained realization. It cuts off all branches.
It is like a creeping vine that has abandoned its rows and furrows, yet does not fall into the realm of emotional consciousness.
I did not expect that while the Great Dharma was in decline, one such as this person could be seen. Qianyan agreed with my words.
What I saw at that time consisted of only one or two chapters. Since then, whether in Wu or Chu, or in Liang, Song, Lu, or Wei, many renowned monks and bodhisattvas [have appeared].
There was one who came to pay his respects upon the Puyang River. Once I had seen him, I immediately asked, "Have you seen the Nantang?

He replied, "I have. I asked, "What did he say? Thereupon, each of us opened our bags to show [the records] to one another. As we saw more and more, our hearts grew to admire them, and our devotion increased all the more.
Later, when I arrived in the capital, his disciple Zu Qin Haishou again brought the records of the three assemblies and presented them to me.
I sought to compose a preface for it and read it over several days, thereby gaining a comprehensive view of its entirety. Alas!

To occupy the lion throne and expound the Dharma of the Tathāgata is a task of no small weight. Were another to undertake this, they would likely plunder here and there from various sources, piecing together fragments into a composition where the traces of the chisel and hammer remain evident.
In the Master’s work, however, all is harmoniously fused without trace, indistinguishable from the source itself.

When clouds drift away, the sky is clear. As for others, they remain confined and stagnant in a single corner; they encounter obstacles at every turn, such that they may achieve something here but ultimately neglect what lies there.
Our Master, however, regarding the pivot of killing and giving life, moves with complete mastery in both vertical and horizontal directions.

When others were in such a state that their spirits were withered and their resolve broken, unable to uplift themselves and thus failing to respond to the inquiries of those seeking instruction, the Master alone remained full and complete, extending his influence to all quarters.
As for one such as the Master, the depth of his realization is truly beyond the measure of ordinary minds.
Indeed, since the coming from the West at Shaolin, there has been nothing but the investigation of the source of the mind.

The words were direct and straightforward, with no concealment from the outset. When the transmission reached Dajian (the Sixth Patriarch), fearing it might be disseminated as mere worldly truth, he could not help but keep it secret and guard it closely.
Through successive generations, eminent masters have risen and fallen according to the times; their compassion was both profound and stern, and each established their own distinct approach.
Although their methods of guidance appear to differ, they all serve to eliminate false conditions and draw beings back [to the truth].

The orthodox path is but one. By the end of the Song dynasty, however, those who sought the extraordinary and pursued the anomalous increasingly abandoned their teachers’ transmissions and drifted toward heterodoxy;
such instances became numerous. When gentlemen speak of this, they cannot help but sigh with deep regret.
You, Master, are able to tread within the bounds of propriety and follow the footsteps of your ancestors, upholding the True Vehicle to enable others to see it once again.
The legacy of the Great Mirror (Da Jian) and his merit in upholding the True Dharma—how could these be considered small? My admiration for the Master has not been a matter of a single day;
I have had the opportunity to examine both his profound and his mundane writings. Thus, I know that the Master’s realization was uniquely deep, such that it cannot be surpassed by others.
Yet, what is truly regrettable is that the Master’s fame and official rank did not equal his virtue, which caused his teachings...
The Dharma covers the Five Mountains; it spreads the dense clouds of compassion and pours down the torrential rain of the teachings.
Thus, its merit extends far and wide, reaching beyond what is seen here and now. Nevertheless, fame is external, whereas virtue is internal. Virtue resides within.

It is not external. The Master values what is internal and regards what is external as light. If one were to judge the elevation or depression of what is internal based on the honor or insignificance of what is external, such a person does not understand the Master.

I have already recorded the Master’s deeds in detail in a completed biography, which has been engraved upon a durable stone. Furthermore, for those who read this record, I have set forth my explanation in this manner. — Qianyan.

Within the light of meditative concentration, it is not necessarily the case that he would not have agreed with my words. His master’s name was Qingyu, his courtesy name was Liaohan, and his style name was Nantang.
He belonged to the Zhu clan and was a native of Linhai in Taizhou. It is said that he once resided at the three Chan monasteries of Kaifu, Benjue, and Lingyan.
Preface by Song Lian (Jingliao), Jinhua, Academician of the Hanlin Academy, Grand Master of the Second Class with the Rank of Assistant Minister of the Household,

The *Shanshu* (Mountain Gate) Commentary states: When a Buddha appears in the world, each sits upon a flower; their reflections meet and their radiance connects, yet they do not borrow from one another.
The *Shanmen* (Gate of the Mountain) Commentary states: There is host and guest, there is response and chant; cutting off the tongue at its root, a single blow serves for both.

"I respectfully offer this single burner of incense for the sake of the Great Monk Gulin, currently presiding at Baoning Chan Temple; I do not seek to repay his virtue or requite his grace."

The Master then looked over the great congregation and said, "This single gathering is no different from Vulture Peak.
Is there anyone here who will exert themselves for the sake of the assembly? A monk asked, "The phoenix of the Cinnabar Mountain has its nine-fold plumage; what is its stage [of attainment]?"
Pure and lofty, he is separated from the five clouds; when the four seas look up to him in full reverence, they wish to hear his true song in response, O Enlightened Ruler.

The Master said: "A thousand peaks pay homage to Mount Hua; ten thousand streams flow solemnly into the vast ocean. The student asked: "When the Way prevails in the myriad regions, all return [to it]."

"O Enlightened Lord," [the student] said, "In a single phrase, there is no private interest; you benefit all sentient beings. The Master said, "The Yellow River has nine bends; its waters originate from Kunlun.
The student asked, "I have already received your instruction regarding the prayers of blessing; as for the matter of the supreme vehicle (*zongmen*), what is it like?

The Master said, "The eyes do not see their own nostrils. The student asked, "The stream of Caoxi is not stagnant water; when a single drop suddenly arrives and a thousand waves compete to rise, at such a time—"
"What? The Master said, "Step back, step back. The monk stepped forward and said, "In my life I have never known how to hide another's virtues;
wherever I go, I speak of Xiangsi to everyone. The Master said, "Do not slander me, monk. Another monk asked, "Heaven does not speak, yet the four seasons proceed;
Earth does not speak, yet the myriad things grow. I, a student, have a doubt; I pray for your instruction. The Master said, "At the place where ten thousand people look up from afar."
"The red sun reaches the heart of heaven. The student said, "The village elder knows nothing of the labors of Yao and Shun; drumming *dong-dong*, they sacrifice to the River God.
The Master said, "Seeing with eyes like one blind; speaking with a mouth like one mute. The student said, "For a thousand ages, beneath the foot of Mount Hua."
Furthermore, adding Pan Lang riding his donkey backward. The Master then gave a shout. The monk bowed. The Master then said:

"To raise the banner of the Dharma, to establish the fundamental tenet, to open wide the unsurpassed wondrous gate, and to reveal the primary truth—what is the sky too vast, and what is the earth too narrow?"
The green mountains are not green; the white clouds are not white. The tipsy old man at the crossroads is wide awake in his dreams;
the stinking monkey in the three-family village possesses such extraordinary elegance. He overturns the nests of right and wrong and cuts off the tracks of the mundane and the sacred.
Under Deshan’s staff, the Great Function is fully revealed; beneath Linji’s shout, there is a wind-like grace that sheds the physical body. With robes trailing, he sits in ease.
Adjusting his robes:
The Sage Son of Heaven continues the transformation of the eras of Tang and Yu; he cultivates civil virtue and lays down arms. The worthy Chancellor pours forth like autumnal rain.

"Setting aside for a moment the fact that this staff pierces through the nostrils of everyone here—what about Liang Baogong riding the Buddha Hall out through the mountain gate?"
"In the end, what has been accomplished? He strikes the meditation staff and says: "A thousand-fathom whale spouts forth as vast waves fly;

Again, citing the Patriarch [Bodhidharma], he said: "I originally came to this land to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. One flower opens into five petals;

the fruiting occurs naturally. Master Wuzu Fayuan said: "Master Bodhidharma walked with his feet and spoke with his mouth as he pleased, yet the descendants of later generations have mostly fallen into calculating deliberation.
Do you all wish to understand the place where the flower opens and the fruit is realized?"
"Pears from Zhengzhou, dates from Qingzhou—among all things, none surpass those that excel in their origin and destination. The Master said:

"I wield the tongs and hammer of one's own fundamental share to shatter the nests of emotional understanding. Even if you were to restore the Five Patriarchs, if you wish to see the place where flowers bloom and fruit ripens, it is still far off.
Do you all wish to understand the place where flowers bloom and fruit ripens? Cast away the pears of Zhengzhou and set down the dates of Qingzhou."

In movement and stillness, in going and coming, he encompasses all yet remains unattached. One withdraws three, two adds four; it cuts through iron and severs nails, blending mud with water.
It has its origin but no fundamental basis. Shattering the ultimate barrier, a thousand blossoms bloom upon the pestle’s tip.
Have you not seen? As the Chan Master Changsha said: "The person sitting atop a hundred-foot pole—though they have gained entry, it is not yet the truth."
With a hundred bamboo poles and a foot heavy at the tip, he takes a step forward; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, his entire body is seen.

Holding up the staff, he says: "Riding a fine steed, galloping atop a high tower; the Milky Way rolls a jade ball across ten thousand miles. He strikes the staff and says: "Sometimes one rides upon the bright moon."
Unaware that he had already crossed over to Cangzhou, [the Master] again cited Deshan’s informal teaching (xiao-can): “I do not answer those who speak; those who ask questions receive thirty blows.
At that time, a monk stepped forward, and Deshan struck him across the back with his staff. The monk said, “I have not even asked a question; why do you strike me? Deshan replied, “You...”
"Where are you from? The monk replied, "A man from Silla. Xishan said, "Before you have even stepped onto the ship's railing, you deserve thirty blows.
Later, Master Yuan of Ciana commented: "That was far too much relying on power to bully others.
As for my own view, I want everyone to know it together. If that monk had been a true man at the time, when he heard him say, 'Where are you from?'"
The man immediately overturned the meditation seat, kicked it up, and walked away.

Even if Deshan’s teeth were like a forest of swords and his mouth like a blood-basin, he would still have had to retreat three thousand paces. Why? Because those who recognize the Dharma are afraid. The Master said:
"Deshan was executing his true command, yet this clever monk failed at the critical juncture. If you say he relied on his power to deceive others, that would be to wrong the former masters."
A little. Nevertheless, do you still know where this old man of the hermitage has ended up? A sword leaves its precious scabbard because of injustice;
medicine emerges from its golden jar to save the sick.

On the occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival, he ascended the hall and raised the following case: Once, while Mazu was enjoying the moon with Xitang, Baizhang, and Nanquan, Mazu asked, "At this very moment, what is it?

Xitang said, "It is precisely the time for making offerings. Baizhang said, "It is precisely the time for practicing cultivation. Nanquan shook his sleeves and walked away. Mazu remarked, "The sutras return to the Tripitaka and Chan returns to the sea; only Puyan alone transcends the mundane world. The Master said: [The Master then added: "Mazu’s words were like a great ocean, vast and deep, yet they did not reach the source. Xitang’s words were like a mountain peak, lofty and steep, yet they did not reach the root. Baizhang’s words were like a river, flowing and winding, yet they did not reach the origin. Only Nanquan’s action was like the sky—unobstructed and pervasive, cutting off all paths and leaving no trace. He alone reached the ultimate source. If you can see it thus, you will know that the Buddhas and patriarchs have never been separate from you; they have merely pointed directly at your own face. If you cannot see it thus, you must examine it thoroughly. Do not let it pass for nothing; do not let it become a mere idle story. If you can understand it right now, you will realize that the moon is always bright and the water is always clear—there is no need to wait for the Mid-Autumn Festival."

It is said that their spirits were in harmony and their capacities responded to one another; throughout past and present, everyone has claimed that this "Discourse on Playing with the Moon" is extraordinary.
Yet they fail to realize that Master Mazu, out of paternal affection for his son, was unconsciously revealing his own flaws.

What character is this? The Master said, "The strokes are distinct. The monk stepped forward and said, "In the past, someone asked Dizang [Bodhisattva], and Dizang replied, 'Look at the commentary below. Now tell me, what is the commentary? (Note: This passage is a classic *gong'an* (public case) from the *Wumen Guan*.

The "character" is a pun on the Chinese word for "not" (*bù*), which can be visually deconstructed into the components "one" (*一*) and "eight" (*八*). The "commentary" refers to the realization that the true meaning lies beyond the literal characters.)
"What do you say about the footnotes? The Master said, "You have not yet understood the footnotes; first look at the main text. The monk asked, "What is the main text?
The Master said, "It does not form the character 'yi' (以), nor is it the character 'ba' (八). The monk said, "Master, please do not deceive people.
The Master said, "How many people have you questioned up until now? The monk said, "I am questioning the Master right now. The Master said, "In that case, it is you who are deceiving me."

the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all contained within the source of the heart. One attains such a state that boundless lands and realms—self and other—are not separated by so much as a hair’s tip;

ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from this very moment of thought. Furthermore, it is said: "As the sun's course shifts and changes, the days grow long toward the south."

"To offer this body and mind to every dust mote and land—this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness."

Small Assembly. Tomorrow is the winter solstice; tonight is the small assembly. The lantern poses a question, and the pillar points the way south.

*Hè!* (A shout). Entering the hall:
"In the School of the Patriarchs there are three phrases: 'Bestowing before the question is even raised. If you further intend to ask 'How is it?'—I know you are far too crude and reckless.

The second phrase is this very person sitting or standing with solemn dignity; to speak of the "Yellow Path" as being different is the third phrase.
What is the first phrase? If you can say it, I grant that you have attained the blessing of the moment.
If you cannot say it, the road is perilous where it is level, and people are busy in their moments of stillness. (He lets out a shout.)
Ascending the hall: Three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. Śākyamuni the Old Man did not know they existed; for six years on the Snowy Mountains, his eyes grew numb and bleary.
He mistook the Southern Dipper for the Northern Dipper. Within a single hair-pore he sees the entire body; across ten billion hair-pores he boasts of being a skilled hand.
Before the hall, the iron saw dances the *Santai*; atop the ridge, the stone man opens a smiling mouth. *Hè!* (A shout).

"Ho! [The Master] ascends the hall. "Last night in the state capital, at the Music Hall, they performed a variety of plays. There were those who were dignified and extraordinary, and there were those who were ugly and unfitting to behold.
Even the ghostly faces and divine heads were quite amusing. But tell me, what was it that was so funny? As I observed..."

The people of this world are like a great farce. As it is said: scholars, warriors, physicians, diviners, officials, farmers, artisans, and merchants—each displaying their own skills while deceiving one another.
When they reach the end of the twelfth lunar month, they suddenly find themselves in a state of total failure.
An observant bystander watches and cannot help but cover his mouth in laughter. He lets out a shout: "The New Year begins its reign; all things are renewed. By the willows on the bank...

Shaking the golden plum blossoms, the jade is broken; throughout the myriad realms, the Great Balance (Hongjun) turns as one vital breath. Descending from the seat, he circulates through the hall for tea.

Ascending the hall, he raises his whisk and says: "Buddha to Buddha, hand is passed to hand; Patriarch to Patriarch, it is transmitted from one to another. There is the partial and the full; there is the biased and the perfect;
there is the empty and the existent; there is the real and the provisional; there is the sudden and the gradual; there is the holy and the ordinary. He strikes [the whisk].
The whisk-broom said: "Ordinary is unattainable; holy is unattainable. Gradual is unattainable;
sudden is unattainable. Expedient means are unattainable; ultimate reality is unattainable. Existence is unattainable; emptiness is unattainable.
Perfection is unattainable; partiality is unattainable. Fullness is unattainable; half is unattainable."
It cannot be attained. Transmission cannot be attained. Bestowal cannot be attained. Ancestor cannot be attained. Buddha cannot be attained.
Even this "cannot be attained" cannot itself be attained. Therefore it is said: "To take it is not possible; to let it go is not possible;
within that which cannot be attained, one simply attains it. To attain it in the mind is like a *yilan* flower becoming a sandalwood tree; to lose it...
To them, the nectar of immortality is but a garden of thorns; the chestnut thorns and the diamond circle—only those who can swallow and pass through them may proceed.
Yet when three by three and two by two, they cannot shake them off; when ten thousand by ten thousand and a thousand by a thousand, they remain stuck.
On this occasion of the Imperial Birthday, for Your Majesty, I shall shatter the double mystery. Do you understand? The imperial pavilion enshrouds purple qi; the golden hall...

"The root of sentient beings returns to its source by relying on the ocean of wisdom; the stream of conscious beings takes the Dharma-body as their essence.

The Buddha ascends the hall for the occasion of his *nirvāṇa*: Before the fifteenth day, the Buddhas do not appear in the world; after the fifteenth day, there is likewise no *nirvāṇa*.
It is precisely on the fifteenth day that willows are green and flowers are red, mountains are bright and waters are azure.
At every turn one sees the splendor beyond kalpas; everywhere is the realm of the Great Man. It is simply a matter of sitting firmly in the light of the present moment, directly beneath.

To know where one returns is already to involve discursive thought; once one engages in such reflection, it becomes a superfluous dharma. Striking the meditation seat, he said: "The bamboo borrowed from the neighboring wall is difficult to separate;
though the boat is precariously tilted, I sit upright within."
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the example of Zen Master Baoning Yong, who addressed the assembly, saying: "The wind whistles through the branches and the rain breaks the clods of earth;

Not understanding, three form a group and four make a troop; they go from village to village, gathering blossoms from the pear and plum trees."

The Flower Seller.

From his midnight flight over the city walls, to his six years on the Snowy Mountains, to his departure from the Bodhi tree to the Deer Park and the Swan Pond—it was all within this very trap.

On Vulture Peak and in the monasteries of the coastal lands, throughout three hundred assemblies, there were horizontal and vertical explanations, direct and indirect explanations, secret and manifest explanations, and spontaneous pronouncements made without being asked.

At the very end, when he held up a single flower, it caused the Golden-Colored Honored One to break into a smile; this entrustment of the Dharma-eye also cannot be contained within the circle of conceptual description.
It cannot be attained. Whether you all believe it or not, you cannot escape the circle. Whether you understand it or not, you cannot escape the circle.

Nevertheless, tell me: does this mountain monk still remain within it or not? (He strikes the whisk.

Small Assembly Sermon. Before the Peak of Shaoshi, one tunes a different melody on the strings; along the path of Caoxi, one knows autumn by the falling leaves.
To let go: clouds arise across the eight directions. To hold fast: the four seas are cut off at the current. Holding up the staff, he said: "It is all upon the tip of this staff. Do you see it?"

Dipping into vinegar. He plants his staff on the platform and descends from the seat.

to call the sun by the name of the moon. Linji and Deshan possess but a single "stake"—they let out a shout!
The monks were looking at one another. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Mount Lu.
The Master said, "Is the Five Elders’ Peak white yet? The monk replied, "It is white. The Master asked, "How old is it? The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "Have you not come from Mount Lu? The monk replied, "Yes. The Master then struck him out.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Before the fifteenth day, water flows cold from the edge of the rocks.
After the fifteenth day, wind comes fragrant from within the flowers. On the fifteenth day itself, it is like a single blade of thatch after the fire has passed;
even an iron snake cannot penetrate it. He let out a shout.
Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month: All phenomena are the radiance of the mind; all conditions are but the clarity of one’s nature.

Fundamentally, there is no person who is deluded or enlightened; it simply requires realization this very day. Alas! Old Gautama, why seek such idle vexation? Leaving the mountain and entering the mountain, you rise up only to fall down again.
Last night, as the stars turned and the celestial cords stretched across the sky, you did not realize your entire body had fallen into the wild grass. *Hè!* (A shout)
"Ha! He ascended the hall, raised his whisk, and said, "Do you see it? If you see it but do not grasp it, it will be difficult to forget for a thousand years. To grasp it is not impossible;
how then do you explain the principle of 'seeing'? Is it that there is a seeing of seeing? Or is it that there is no seeing?"
Do you see? Is it not seeing by means of seeing that is neither existent nor non-existent? Is it not seeing by means of seeing that is neither not-existent nor not-non-existent?
If it were thus, you would still not have attained the status of even a servant to that Master. Therefore it is said: "To see clearly, there is not a single thing;
there is no person and there is no Buddha. The great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean. All...

The sages and worthies were like a flash of lightning. O virtuous practitioners of Chan! Lingdao sat through seven broken bundles of *pútuán* grass mats until, at the very moment the curtain was lifted, he suddenly attained realization.
He then said: "How very strange! How very strange! When the curtain is rolled up, one sees the whole world.
If someone asks me what school I understand, I pick up my whisk and strike them right on the mouth. This is the ancient [tradition].

Ascending the hall, he held up one thing and let go of another. A master of the fundamental school covers the earth and heaven; such a peerless adept is rarely encountered.

After the rain falls over the wild pond, the spring water is deep. He threw down the staff and descended from the seat."

Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "The direct transmission of the single lineage has already involved the realms of departure and subtlety. Having cut off all manifold distinctions, I ask the Master to provide an answer.
The Master said: "A broken mirror does not reflect again; fallen flowers cannot return to the branch. The monk pressed further: "Is there no expedient means? The Master said: [Silence].
"A tortoise drills through a broken wall. The Master then said: "The direct pointing of the single transmission precisely involves transcendence and subtlety.

To sit and cut off all manifold differences is to fall into a well with one's eyes open. He raised his staff and struck once: "A tortoise drills through a broken wall; a rooster cries at the fifth watch."
Ascending the hall, Master Dou-shui Yue said: "Tearing through the weeds and observing the wind are done only for the sake of seeing one's nature.
Now, where is this superior man’s nature? Only by recognizing one’s own nature can one escape birth and death. When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, how does one escape?
If you can escape birth and death, you will know the place of departure. When the four elements separate, to what place do you go? (He laughed heartily.)
The assembly: First, there is the proclamation; first, there is the instruction. This is indeed direct and unimpeded.
To truly transcend birth and death, one must awaken to one’s own fundamental mind and see one’s own original nature. I venture to ask you all: what is this nature? What is this mind?
Ultimately, what form does it take? Is it blue, or yellow, or white, or black? Is it long, or short, or large, or small?
Upon hearing such an explanation, some will immediately say: "It is neither blue nor yellow, neither white nor black."

Neither long nor short, neither large nor small—it resembles it, yet it is not yet it. This is what is called "the dwarf watching the play," merely following others up and down; what use is there in that?
One whose eyes are intimate with the truth and who can discern it with their own hands should point it out right here for all to see.
First, it demonstrates that the eye of study is correct; second, it shows that there are people within the monastic community; third, it shows that [the Dharma] can be transmitted.
To open the minds of future students and ensure that the ancestral life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs remains unbroken—does anyone have it?
Does anyone? If not yet, listen to this verse: Nine months of practice pass in a single month; how can one’s diligent investigation be measured by time?
Do not disdain my old and clumsy persistence in exhortation; those who die in vain and live in delusion are exceedingly many. Take care!
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "When one ox drinks water, five horses do not neigh. What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "Familiar faces fill the world;
how many can truly know the heart? The monk pressed further: "When beckoning from across the river, he immediately strides crosswise.
Ultimately, what kind of eye is this? The Master said: "Do not slander Gao Ting. The monk bowed, and the Master continued: "The mind is not yet understood."
The Seal of the Ground. It is difficult to penetrate the Patriarch’s Barrier. To wish to penetrate the Patriarch’s Barrier, one must clarify the Seal of the Mind-Ground.
[He] holds up his staff and says, "This is not the Seal of the Mind-Ground. [He] strikes the ground with the staff and says, "This is not the Patriarch’s Barrier.

If you can clarify it and penetrate it, then the entire Great Canon—its five thousand and forty-eight fascicles, its provisional and ultimate, its partial and perfect, its expedient and real, and its emptiness and existence—is not worth a single [stroke].
“Strike! Zhuo struck his staff once. “A three-legged donkey trots about, kicking up its heels; it tramples the universe to pieces until not a square inch of earth remains.

"Ho! Master Zhigong is no ordinary monk. He ascended the hall.

even the grasses, trees, insects, and creatures alike are equally moistened by the Emperor’s bounty. Reaching this point, one cannot say that it is not known, yet not permitted.
It is not that one knows it and yet harbors it; it is vast and boundless, beyond the power of naming. How brilliantly pure it is, worthy of the highest esteem!
What is called the "entrustment upon the Spirit Mountain" lies precisely here. With this single phrase fully raised, let everyone offer their realization.
Do you understand thoroughly? The wondrous power of the great forge existed before heaven and earth; leaf by leaf, flower by flower, all is spring.
The case is cited again. Emperor Tongguang said to Master Xinghua, "I have acquired a treasure in the Central Plains, yet no one is willing to offer a price for it.
Xinghua said, "Lend me a look at it for a moment. The Emperor then lifted up the brim of his head-wrap (*fodou*) and showed it to him.
Huachun said, "The treasure of a sovereign—dare anyone bid its price? The Master said, "Using a broken awl to probe the veins of the earth.
Later, Xuedou said, "If it were not for Huachun being a true adept, by now he would have paid a high price. The Master said, "Gazing upward with bared brows toward the rising sun.
Does Benjue have any excellence? Listen to this verse: "Striking out the five-colored marrow of the phoenix, Beating [the drum]..."
He shattered the bright moon-jewel of the black dragon; beneath the foot of Mount Hua for a thousand ages, there could have been none other than Pan Lang riding his donkey backward.
I have stood before you, honored official, for some time; I humbly pray that you will take care of yourself.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Master Songyuan, who addressed the assembly, saying: "The ancients said: 'When lifted up, heaven turns and earth revolves;
when set down, grass bows and the wind blows. I, Yeshu, am not like this: when lifted up, heaven and earth are pitch-black;
when set down, tiles and pebbles emit light. If suddenly there is one or half a person who, all at once, strikes the top of their head wide open, then Bodhidharma..."
"One school remains desolate. The Master said, "Old Songyuan saw only the sharpness of the chisel's tip, but did not see the squareness of the chisel's head.
Shoushan said, "It is not so with me. When I pick it up, clouds rise over South Mountain; when I set it down, rain falls on North Mountain. What is it like when neither picking up nor setting down?
"Three-tiered waves high, the fish transforms into a dragon; yet the foolish man still uses a bucket to bail out water at night."
Dangshui. Descending from the seat.
On the occasion of dispersing the Green Sprouts Assembly, he ascends the hall and says: "For forty-nine years, there was no dharma that could be spoken.

Throughout the teachings of this lifetime, they have turned like jade and revolved like pearls. Those who penetrate through do not linger on either side; those who cannot penetrate are bound by their own ropes."—Shoushan.
There is a living path to be traveled together with all of you. Raising his whisk, he said: "Do you see it?
From the Deer Park at the beginning, to the Vārāṇasī River at the end—within this interval, dense clouds spread forth, completely covering the trichiliocosm.
Their moisture falls everywhere, saturating the entire land. As for the mountains, rivers, steep valleys, and the flora produced in their secluded depths..."
The forests and groves, the various medicinal herbs, the sugarcane and grapes, and the hundred grains and crops—all are fully abundant.
How fortunate they are! Yet, for no reason at all, Yunmen’s fan in his hand leaps up into the sky, striking the nostrils of Śakra.
A carp from the Eastern Sea receives a blow, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin. (He strikes the whisk and says: "A brocade spread upon brocade."
Another layer of flowers.
Upon receiving the news of the passing of Master Xibai Baoguo, he ascended the hall and said: "When one has not yet realized that objects are but mind, various kinds of discrimination arise.
Once one realizes that objects are but mind, discrimination no longer arises. Within this state where no discrimination arises, the original face is revealed alone."
The Eye. It is simply to be free from marks and names, absolute and beyond all relativity, shattering the dust and piercing the target, penetrating form and penetrating sound.
Thus, my Master Baoguo attained this samādhi; dwelling in mountains at two locations, he transmitted the authentic seal alone, sweeping away erroneous interpretations and upholding this school.
Having completed his great task, he let go of his hands over there; in his final act of total presentation, he was truly radiant.
Cai: Now tell me, when he rubbed his chest and addressed the assembly, and displayed his two feet within the outer coffin—were these the same or different? Striking the meditation seat, he said:
"When the wild sheep hang from the horns, they are atop a thousand peaks; yet there is another wild sheep atop that peak."

A Small *Chanshi* for the End of the Summer Retreat: In the past, there was never anything bound; now, what need is there to untie it? Since binding and untying are fundamentally without mind, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
If you act thus, thus, the myriad phenomena of the forested universe are utterly solitary and precarious; the great earth, its mountains and rivers, are all steep and perilous from top to bottom.
If you do not act thus, thus, beneath the Gate of the Great Sun, every day is like the third autumn month, and the bright moon...
In the hall, throughout the three months of summer, it is thus; yet within this "thusness" there is "not thus," and within "not thus" there is "thus.
All-encompassing wisdom penetrates without obstruction: taking the lantern and placing it inside the Buddha Hall, and setting up the mountain gate upon the lantern.
I ask you, the assembly: within these ninety days, have you attained resonance with this or not? If you have not yet done so, then listen to the Mountain [Master].
The monk, however, had a skillful means. He suddenly took up his staff, struck it once, and said: "A gust of west wind comes; two or three leaves fall.
He then raised another case:
When Mingzhao was traveling on pilgrimage, he arrived at the place of Master Tan of Xingjiao in Quanzhou. As Tan was ascending the hall, he said:
"A traveling man of high caliber must reach the place where the 'whole person' resides; he must also reach the place where the 'half-person' resides.
Mingzhao then asked, "I do not ask about the place where the whole person resides; what is the place where the half-person resides? Tantan was speechless.
Later, he instead had his junior disciple ask Mingzhao, "What is the place where the half-person resides? Mingzhao said, "If you wish to know..."
"Where does the 'half-person' reside? He is merely a fellow who plays with lumps of mud. Master Ying’an commented: "I have heard of the One-Eyed Dragon;
indeed, he possesses but a single eye. Today, if a monk were to suddenly ask, 'What is the place where the half-person resides?
I would strike him across the back with my staff. If he asked further, 'What is the place where the whole person resides? I would likewise strike him."

He drove him out. Why? Because "if one does not do it once, one will not stop at two. The Master said, "They are both fellows playing with lumps of mud; yet Old Man Ying’an was slightly superior. He then composed another verse and presented it to the assembly: "Xingjiao upholds [the truth] and is not deceived; [The verse continues as follows:

The old man of the West has long since passed away; How can you still speak of 'before' and 'after'? If you wish to know the meaning of this matter, Look at the staff in the hands of the monk from Dongshan. Xingjiao upheld [the teaching] and was not deceived.
Mingzhao followed the custom of playing with the mudball; the eye upon the staff is as bright as the sun. To recognize true gold, one must look within the fire.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "Dongshan said, 'In early autumn and late summer, going east or west, you must head toward where there is not a single thing for ten thousand miles.'"
"A single blade of grass is nowhere to be found. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Forged from solid steel, cast from raw iron.
The student asked further, "As for Shishuang hearing this and saying, 'Why not say that as soon as one goes out the door, it is already grass'—how about that? The Master said:
"One is a clumsy fellow; one is a Fukienese. The Master then said: "Before the fifteenth day, it is the bottom-piercing diamond circle;
after the fifteenth day, it is the swallowed thorn-bush fruit. On the very fifteenth day, the mouth of the cloth bag is untied, and the path for the patch-robed monks is open.
He struck his staff and said: "All stars bow toward the North; there is no water that does not flow [to the sea]."

Facing East. On the Mid-Autumn Festival, guests ascended the hall. At Vulture Peak, the moon was pointed out; at Caoxi, the moon was discussed. Mazu, Baizhang, Xitang, and Nanquan all gazed upon the moon.
Panshan said: "The mind-moon is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the myriad phenomena. The light does not illuminate the object; the object..."
Nor does it exist. When both light and its object have vanished, what thing is there? A mangy horse tied to a withered post. Dongshan said:
"When light and its object have not yet vanished, what thing is there? A black ox lying in dead water. Master Yuyang said: "The moon in the water cannot be fished up;
one’s labor is in vain as one shatters the sky reflected in the water. At night, deep in the mountain temple, they open the door and sleep; the moon itself—"
Suddenly appearing before me, you have exhausted your own mind and laughed the mouths of others to pieces. Today is the Mid-Autumn Festival of Original Enlightenment;
a guest from Mount Ling has come to visit. It happens that the sky is filled with wind and rain.

Since there is nothing to practice and nothing to offer as an act of devotion, I shall certainly not brush off my sleeves and depart. Instead, we cannot help but lean together against the precarious railing and rest upon the curved balustrade. Pushing...
A single wheel appears before one’s face; its pure radiance extends ten thousand *li*. Without establishing the three barriers, he opens the way for humans and devas;
by suddenly eliminating the four propositions, he glorifies the ancestral path. (Striking the whisk) "The eighty-four thousand are not merely phoenix feathers;
thirty-three men have entered the tiger’s den."

Ascending the hall for the opening of the furnace: The ancient mirror—its breadth and narrowness; the brazier—its depth and shallowness. There is not a single piece of firewood or charcoal, yet its radiance extends ten thousand fathoms.
There is no talk of host or guest, so there is no need for deliberation; the spiritual mechanism of killing and giving life—why bother to proclaim it? Speech is deception, silence is slander.
Beyond speech and silence, there is a matter that remains. A cow in Huai state eats grain; a horse in Yi state suffers from a bloated belly. Heaven...
He went down to seek out a physician. He applied moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig, let out a roar, and descended from his seat.

At the memorial service for the Patriarch, he offered incense: "His practice and realization were in accord; both the school and its teachings were mastered. His vision emptied the four seas; his spirit exhaled a long rainbow."
Before leaving the Western Region, I longed for a thorough beating; now that I have come to this Eastern Land, let us simply tolerate one another. One flower opens into five petals;
each receives its share of the spring breeze.
When the guest ascends to the hall: "The Western Arrival of Bodhidharma did not establish written words; he pointed directly at the human mind, enabling one to see their nature and become a Buddha.
These words are known by all people. Yet, as for the Great Canon of teachings—its five thousand and forty-eight volumes—how is it?

Whether this is the Buddha speaking or Māra speaking, you will certainly attain liberation. It does not matter if you merely echo the empty sounds within a small jade gong or stir up dust and grit atop the Lapis Lazuli Hall;
take up the three strips of bamboo and bind them around your belly, then go to dwell among the mountains wherever you may be.
If this is not yet the case, then listen as the staff of Shoushan manifests its divine transformations. (He plants his staff. Golden hammer!
The shadow moves; the light of the precious sword is cold. A single arrowhead pierces the three barriers at will. Xie Lang is not on his fishing boat.
[He] ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "The mountain in front of you. The monk pressed further, "I do not ask about the Dharma; what is a monk?
The Master said, "Three heads and two faces, detested by all. The monk bowed. The Master then asked [the monk]:
The monk asked, "What is the Dharma? The monk replied, "Next year there will be new branches; the wind of spring disturbs all, never ceasing.
The Master said, "It is too late to ask about your transgression. The Master then said, "If you do not bring it forth when we meet, one knows it exists as soon as the intention arises."
Turning back the pivot at the very source, he lets out a great lion’s roar. He unfolds the donkey’s feet and extends the Buddha’s hand;
grasping the vajra mallet, he shatters all old nests and traps. How do the lands of the East and the West compare? Looking at each one, they are like the sun in midday.

The Master said, “A hundred-foot well before the mountains of Huayin. The student asked, “What is it like after seeing it? The Master said, “An eternal pine atop Mount Zhurong.
The student asked, “Setting aside these two paths, I wish to hear the essential teaching. The Master said, “Do not take the intellectual learning of the idle and bury the mind of the Patriarch.
The Master then said, “The very life of the Buddhas of the past and the governing principles of the Buddhas of the future are both contained within this.”

If you hold fast, the six sense-aggregates will block all openings; if you let go, the single Yang will be restored. I shall not speak of shoots bursting through stone, nor of flowers blooming on an iron tree;
I simply instruct the practitioners to strike the drum for the informal discourse (*xiaocan*), so as to spare everyone from their collective drowsiness.
Do you understand? If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of themselves; if the mind does not waver, the myriad dharmas [are stilled].

It is all one and the same. To lift Mount Sumeru on a scale and weigh it at two *liang*, selling it cheaply in the east and selling it dearly in the west—no matter how authentic a monk may be, when faced with this, there is no way to discern it.
Have you not seen how Linji asked Huangbo about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Three times he was struck with sixty blows of the staff, as if they were merely the brushing of a *haozhi* (moss twig) fan. And yet, when it came down to...
On the banks of the Gaoyuan River, he immediately understood where he was returning.
Xinghua said, "When I traveled throughout the South, I never once struck upon a single person who truly understood the Buddha-dharma with the tip of my staff.
When I arrived before the hall of Dajue, I took off my patched robe and received a severe beating; it was at that moment that I personally saw the late Master Linji at Huangbo."
The meaning behind Huangbo’s eating the staff: O Zen masters, to meet blow for blow with full force is not yet to be a true adept;
to carve a boat after a sword has fallen is hardly fit for serious discourse. Nevertheless, had he not shot the stone tiger at Lantian, he might well have killed General Li by mistake.
Again, it was raised: National Teacher Wuye said, "If even a single hair’s worth of ordinary or saintly thoughts has not been exhausted, one will inevitably enter the womb of a donkey or a horse.
Master Baiyun Cuan said, "Even if every single hair’s worth of ordinary or saintly thoughts were purified away..."

"Nor can one avoid entering the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse. The Master said, "If even a single hair’s worth of ordinary or holy thoughts has not been exhausted, then it is certainly true that one enters the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse.
But when even a single hair’s worth of ordinary or holy thoughts is completely purified, why does one still enter the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse?
To see 'No-Action' is easy; to see 'White Clouds' is difficult. *Du!* (A blow with the staff. Understand!"
There is no need for a double-edged sword; why seek the "Nine-Return Elixir" to prolong one's life?
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Nanquan slew the cat; Zhaozhou came out wearing straw sandals. Xinghua engaged in a battle of dharma;
Kebin served the steamed rice and then departed. All these were manifestations of the innate spiritual radiance, yet fundamentally they did not borrow the nostrils of another."
He lets out a breath. "The reason is this: yesterday, when the Head Seat preached the Dharma, he towered above gods and men;
this morning, as my fellow practitioners passed by, they brought forth the eye of the school. But tell me, what business does this mountain monk accomplish with these two flaps of skin?
He strikes the meditation seat. "No one has recognized the merit of his past labor on the battlefield; he simply wishes to re-examine his epoch-making achievements."

Ascending the hall on the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month: Two thousand years ago, before Mount Zhengjue (Vimalakīrti), when the morning star appeared, Śākyamuni Buddha attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
Two thousand years later, within Mount Benjue (Original Enlightenment), as the morning star appears now, this assembly of mine—
"What have you accomplished? [The Master] lets out a shout. "If you awaken, there is no need to apply effort; when concentration and wisdom are perfectly luminous, one does not linger in emptiness.
The stream flows from the eastern ravine to the western ravine; charcoal is burned on the southern mountain while the northern mountain glows red."
At the request of the deceased official Quan Xinpu, the Master presided over a small assembly for the memorial service. After the questions and answers were concluded, the Master said:

"The Land of the Mind is revealed in its majestic presence; the Amitābha of one's own nature is not hidden. With a sudden opening of the eye of the thousand sages right here and now, where else would you seek the Western Paradise?
Therefore it is said: 'If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season. Time and season..."
If you arrive, the principle will manifest of itself. Now that the time has arrived, how do you explain this principle of "manifesting of itself"?

Is it the matter of deeply grieving for one's parents and their arduous labors in raising you? Is it the matter of resigning from office, declining emolument, and providing simple food and water to bring them joy?
Is it the matter of being careful in funeral rites and honoring the distant past, cherishing the repayment of their boundless kindness?
Is it this? Is it that which transcends birth and death and crosses to the other shore?

Is it that which exhausts retribution in the Sahā world and gives rise to conditions for the Pure Land? Is it that which takes refuge in the lotus pedestal and beholds the Buddha as the flower blooms?
Is it that upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, one realizes the patience of non-arising?
Is it that having attained this patience, one then contemplates the salvation of sentient beings? Is it that when merit is perfected and fruition is complete, one attains the Bodhi of Buddhahood?
Is it that once what was to be done has been accomplished, one enters Parinirvāṇa? Be glad to know that these have nothing to do with it. Old Śākyamuni!
The Way of the Son: In a single thought-moment, universally contemplate immeasurable kalpas; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding.

Thus one thoroughly understands the matters of the three periods of time and transcends all expedient means to achieve the Ten Powers. If you awaken here, you will know how to establish the Dharma and destroy the Dharma.
All are called nirvana. Wisdom and folly are both equally prajñā. The dharmas accomplished by bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists are the same as bodhi.
Ignorance and suchness are no different realms. All precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms, as well as lust, anger, and ignorance—[are all one].
All are the Brahma-conduct; the hells and the celestial palaces are all pure lands. Those with nature and those without nature alike attain the Buddha-way.
Thus, the late Lady An Rushi Miaoshan—eighty-two years ago—was originally never born.
Eighty-two years later, that which was extinguished was never truly extinguished; free from the two conditions of arising and ceasing, the long sky shines with the single moon.
Thus it is with Mother Anren; thus it is with Lady Qian. Thus it is with Lady Qian; thus it is with the assembly gathered here now.
Thus it is with the assembly gathered here now; so it is throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm. If...
Whether saint or ordinary person, whether monastic or layperson, whether male or female, and including both sentient and insentient beings—all are likewise thus.

Such a Dharma has been secretly transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs; do not differentiate between self and other, for there is no distinction between self and other. The Way of the Dharma King is vast and boundless.
Good assembly, when purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates through; in silent illumination, it encompasses empty space. Return then to observe the world.
In an instant, it is like a dream-event. The Buddhas of the three periods of time are a dream; the six generations of patriarchs are a dream;
the old monks of the world are a dream; the great assembly before you is a dream. That which is born is a dream; that which dies is non-existence.
That which speaks is a dream; that which listens is a dream. True Suchness and liberation are dreams; Bodhi and Nirvana are dreams. There is nothing.
To clarify: afflictions are a dream; the saṃsāra of the six realms is a dream. When the dream is shattered, there is not a single thing of worldly toil remaining.

"A scorched brick strikes one who is frozen to the marrow. At such a time, as for those two people, An and Ren—who are uniquely liberated and without dependence—how would you express that transcendent, surpassing phrase?
He strikes the whisk and says: "The lands tremble to welcome Śākyamuni."
Lotuses of jewels fill the air as they escort Guanyin.
Entering the hall: Today is the fifteenth day of the first month; Mount Shouyan plucks the poor and makes them wealthy, illuminating the heart-lamp of the full moon.
He eclipses the myriad stars along the celestial path. This is not merely to celebrate the Lantern Festival with the two orders of the assembly, both senior and junior;
it is also to express gratitude to the Abbot Yunfeng for his far-reaching and diligent visit. Suddenly, he picks up his staff, strikes once, and says:
"Beyond the curtain of the bright night, the *Santai* dance unfolds; there is another mechanism that restores the Buddhas and Patriarchs. He gives a shout.

A Small Memorial Lecture for Master Jiang, the Recluse of Xuánxué. The Dharma-body is formless, adorning itself by gathering all virtues;
the Dharma-eye is flawless, penetratingly illuminating all capacities. Through it, the Three Vehicles are established; from it, the five natures are distinguished.
It opens the gates of the provisional and the real, the sudden and the gradual, and cuts off the path of the cycle of birth and death. Transcending high...
Transcending all things, it wondrously emerges before sound; it is that which the profound cannot fathom and that which learning cannot master.
Though dwelling within the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*), it manifests the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) without destroying the characteristics of the conditioned;

though dwelling within the realm of the unconditioned, it manifests the conditioned dharma without discriminating the nature of the unconditioned. Thus, it can ferry the four types of birth across and serve as a bridge and vessel for the nine realms of existence.

In the human realm there is no fixed place; when meeting with a shout, do not raise it too often. Those who have attained realization must know the secret shock.
Entering the hall, he said: "One is raised and the three are made clear; the eye and the scale are precise. At the summit of the ten-thousand-fathom peak, the snowy waves are burst asunder.

The Gandharva King plays music, and the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all become the sound of the lute. It reaches such a point that Mount Sumeru stands towering and the waters of the sea [surge]."
The waves surged; Kāśyapa rose to dance. The World-Honored One testified: "As for you all, why have you been dozing so consistently?
He let out a shout and descended from his seat.

Small Session (Xiaocan). The golden crow flies and the jade hare runs; as summer passes and winter comes, all remains as it was. Not involving the conditions of spring, there is another way. Today is the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month.
From patriarch to patriarch it has been transmitted; from Buddha to Buddha they have handed it down. When one phrase is fully raised, ten thousand functions are penetrated.

Pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Now tell me: is this the primary meaning, or is it the secondary meaning?
You bhikṣus, having reverently received the imperial decree and been granted the imperial incense, within these seven days, the three wheels have turned together.

I once asked about this meaning; now I have nothing to say, and you likewise have nothing to hear. This absence of speech and hearing is called "one meaning" and "two meanings.
With doors and windows wide open, ten thousand miles are not hung with a single cloud. The wind of Yao sweeps vast and clear; the sun of Shun shines bright and warm.
The traveler yields the path to the plowman; the plowman yields the boundary to the traveler. Now, for the sake of this festive praise of the fast, how would you say it?
"Lifting the unperforated flute of Shaolin, everyone blows forth ten-thousand-year joy."
Again, it is recounted: When the King of East India invited the Patriarch Prajñātāra for a meal, he asked, "Everyone here recites the sutras;

[The text] consists of one or two fascicles. The Master said: "The Great King falls where the ground is heavy; the Venerable One pierces where the material is thin. I, this mountain monk, am not like that.

"I pray Your Majesty will cast down the mirror of heavenly discernment. Even if one forgets the fish-trap after catching the fish, the entrustment of Vulture Peak remains intact.
Do you understand this thoroughly? To watch archery and hunting from atop the imperial palace tower is not the same as clearing a field of weeds.

To see [the truth]—if no one preaches the Buddha-dharma, even those with wisdom cannot comprehend it.
Mount Shou does not spare his vast, billowing mouth of thirty-six thousand qing from Lake Taihu, nor his towering tongue of seventy-one peaks of Mount Dongting;

he has already spoken, speaks now, and shall speak. In this perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), there is no obstruction to the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*); in this sequential arrangement, there is no obstruction to the perfect interfusion. Borrowing the "Póshān" [robe].
The disciple bows to the Master’s age. A frog at the bottom of the well swallows the moon.
[The Master] strikes the whisk and ascends the hall: "To clarify the mind through form and manifest the principle through phenomena—donkeys bray like donkeys and dogs bark like dogs.

Provisional and ultimate, emptiness and existence: hiding one's body beneath the water, yet being burned by fire. Each and every one looks southward at the Northern Dipper. (He plants his staff.

Entering parinirvāṇa, he beats the Dharma drum atop Mount Longevity. If the great assembly says the World-Honored One has passed into extinction, they slander the Buddha;

He reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, causing all sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

in rolling up and unfolding, one establishes the heaven and earth beyond the square. Not thus, not thus: in extending and intersecting, one hangs the sun and moon within the realm.

Jin said, "Why did the National Teacher, on the contrary, say: 'I thought I had failed you; it turns out you have failed me'?
The Master said, "A cangue upon his head and shackles upon his feet. Jin said, "Bo Ya and Ziqi were no ordinary acquaintances.

Where can one seek the mind? It overturns the ocean of the hidden treasury and separately proclaims the profound resonance. While in all other quarters they merely watch as the oxen eat grass, here one practices within one’s own monastic grove.
One does not speak of "betraying me" or "betraying you," nor does one speak of "illuminating the past" or "illuminating the present.

Only the single thought-moment of resonance is valued; naturally, the myriad objects of perception subside into stillness. As the Fifth Patriarch said: "It is like two horses locking horns in combat."
Like a flash of lightning, meeting brings great wealth and honor; failing to meet, one faces emptiness. (He lets out a shout.
Entering the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony: does the assembly still see Old Śākyamuni? Before leaving Tuṣita Heaven, his face was covered in dust;
once born from his mother’s womb, his entire body was smeared with mud. Even if you take the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the grasses, trees, and forests—all of them...
For the sake of patch-robed monks: every single monk possesses immeasurable ladles, and within each ladle lies an immeasurable ocean of fragrant water.
From this very day, were one to wash until the end of kalpas, would one ever attain purity?

Here, with eyes clear and hands ready, turn the ladle upside down and you shall see that the marks of defilement are forever departed and the ten directions are pure. If this is not yet so, then listen! (The Master) laughed.
"Kālacitta, there are immeasurable transgressions; this mountain monk also has immeasurable transgressions. These do not concern the affairs of others.
[The assembly] descends from their seats. This is the third time since I came to Jiahe that I have preached the *an-gu* (summer retreat) for you all."

The Dharma. O great assembly! Where incense smoke rises and where lamps and candles shine together, when the Dharma drum sounds, humans and devas gather from all quarters—yet they immediately disperse.
On the Han-yuan Hall, what "Chang'an" can one seek? Before the hall of the Ancient Buddha, at this very moment, the inquiry is complete.
Wait further for me to speak of the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, citing the ancients and the present, and remaining steadfast like a wax figure, guarding [the truth] as a goose guards its snow;
this would be nothing short of a great humiliation for all people. Even if you were to twist your face, extend your hairy hands, and tear down the den of the wild foxes—
To overturn the thicket of thorns is also to abandon oneself to follow others. To seek life by cutting off one's own head—this cannot be done, nor can it not be done.
There is no dharma before the eyes; the intent lies right before the eyes, yet it is not a dharma of the present moment.

this one shout of mine is like a probing pole and a blade of grass; this one shout of mine does not function as a single shout, transcending the sentiments of both sages and ordinary beings."
Exhausted; subject and object are both forgotten. One takes up a single blade of grass and makes it the sixteen-foot golden body;
one takes the sixteen-foot golden body and makes it a single blade of grass. Thus it may be so, and yet thus it may not be so. I dare ask the assembly:
why was it not permissible just now, and why is it permissible now? Is "permissible" or "not permissible" right or wrong? A deviation of a mere hair’s breadth— ...and the error is vast.

When it comes to not bowing to Maitreya, what then? It is enough simply to say: "Sit for now and drink tea. Ultimately, is this a reward or a punishment?

Ascending the hall, he said: "This morning, at the beginning of the summer retreat, I shall establish for you three articles of law: first, one meal a day;
second, one sleep at night; third, whether walking east or west at the mountain gate or within the Buddha hall, you must not tread upon the monastery’s bricks.
He struck his staff and descended from the seat.

One day, while the Master was sitting in his quarters, a monk said, "In the hall, several brothers are reciting the 'Dharma-body Verse on Wearing White Cloth Pants' by Master Huihao, each offering their own interpretation.
I do not know whether they have captured your meaning or not. The Master replied, "What fine news!"
"Let us take it up and see. After the monk had presented each case one by one, the Master said, "If you scold me, I’ll let you have the edge of my tongue;

if you spit at me, I’ll let you have a splash of water. If you wish to understand this verse on the Dharmakāya, you must study for another thirty years. The monk said, "Is that which I am asking right now the Dharmakāya or the Rūpakāya?
The Master said, "A fellow who trails behind donkeys and horses! The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "A fellow who trails behind donkeys and horses!"
"Han! Why are you crying out so wildly? He then struck him.

Entering the hall for discourse, he said: "Fine drizzles of plum rain drench the perilous heights; in the fifth month, the mountain chamber is cold as ice. Do not say that heaven and earth have violated their great trust;
it is simply because you have not yet clarified the mind-ground that it feels like a steaming cauldron. Old Xuedou was much like one who sells flour along with the bran—precious indeed.

At one time, when the primordial awakening was near and the joyful rain was about to fall, the sound of thunder vibrated with joy. Holding up his staff, he said: "Last night, Old Wood Seat addressed me, saying: 'Tomorrow I shall host a family banquet for you all. First, to celebrate this fine rain; second, to warm the assembly;

and third, to twist the nostrils of the monks throughout the world.'* He struck the ground with the staff. *Note: "Twist the nostrils" (捩正鼻孔) is a Zen idiom signifying the act of bringing others to a state of realization or correcting their fundamental understanding. "Old Wood Seat" (木上座) refers to the wooden man (木人) that stands as a symbol of the unchanging, enlightened nature.

The "family banquet" (家燕) implies an intimate gathering within the lineage. The "joyful rain" (喜雨) is a traditional term for timely rain that brings relief and prosperity. The "primordial awakening" (本覺) refers to the inherent Buddha-nature. The "sound of thunder" (雷聲) represents the dynamic power of the Dharma. The striking of the staff (卓) is a gesture of decisive action and transmission.
Holding up his staff, he said, "Do not resent my lack of refinement. I pray you take care. He then descended from the seat.
In the meditation hall, he asked a monk, "I strike you whether you can speak or not. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
He asked another monk, "Do you think they deserved a beating? As the monk was about to open his mouth, the Master struck him out.
He then asked another monk, "Were those two monks who were just beaten right? The monk replied, "Yes. The Master struck him out as well.
Ascending the hall: The myriad phenomena of the forested universe are all sealed by this One Dharma. In the kingdom of Silla, the drum is beaten;
in the Great Yuan Empire, the hall is ascended. When the Dragon King of Lake Anavatapta invited the Buddha for a meal, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bharadvāja was also included among the number.
Ascending the hall, he looked over the assembly and said, "Can you simply rest here like this? As the assembly hesitated, he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall again, he said, "Within the treasury of Vairocana, there is a great scripture. The primary and its attendants are mutually fused; principle and phenomena are both manifest.
Yet when it comes to reading it aloud and opening its chapters, most fail to find the head. The Mountain Gate protects the green sprouts; for your sake, I shall lift them up."
[He repeats this] once. He plants his staff upright, then joins his palms and says: "I prostrate to Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra;
you must surely fulfill the one hundred and forty vows. He then descends from his seat.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "A single leaf falls and the world knows autumn; this everyone knows. A single mote of dust arises and the great earth is gathered in—set this aside for now and do not ask.
To mount the Holy Monk and trample upon Shaokang [Water-lao]—what kind of function is this? He struck his staff and said:
"The dragon gives birth to a golden phoenix chick, which pierces through the azure lapis lazuli."
Small Assembly. Ten thousand miles, not an inch of grass; once you step out the gate, it is all grass. The Great Elephant of Jiazhou suddenly flips over;

the Iron Ox of Shanfu is startled into a collapse. Not appearing before people—selling a dog while hanging up a sheep. Once the mirror is shattered, heaven and earth grow old. To say "it is so" is for gold and sand to be mixed;
to say "it is not" is for jade and stone to be burned together. Without the hammer and tongs of one’s own true portion, how can this be?
It is difficult to clarify the single upper orifice. Holding up his staff, he said: "A single tune on the unperforated flute of Shaolin;
from of old, it has mostly been blown against the wind.
When the head monks were about to enter the hall, [the Master] said: "Within the School of the Patriarchs, there are four types of guest and host. Great Master Linji has already experienced them..."

Pointing this out: if you can discern each and every detail before even stepping through the door, not only will you soon become a master who leads the assembly, but you will also truly be a "grass for our own house.
However, if you cannot distinguish between master and servant, nor differentiate between jade and stone, you have not yet attained the status of a monk.
Have you not seen how when National Teacher Zhong was sleeping, Danxia arrived just then?
He then asked the attendant Tan-yuan, "Is the National Teacher present? Yuan replied, "He is indeed present; it is simply that he does not see guests.
Yun-hua remarked, "That is far too remote. Yuan said, "Do not say so, Venerable; even with the Buddha-eye, one cannot see him. Yun-hua said, "The dragon begets a dragon;
the phoenix begets a phoenix. He then departed. When the National Teacher awoke from his sleep, Yuan recounted the previous conversation to him.
The National Teacher struck him twenty blows with his staff and drove him out. Hearing this, Danxia said, "He is not falsely called the National Teacher of Nanyang.

He gave a shout and said, "He does not know how to be a guest; he troubles the host for no reason. Nevertheless, were it not for the wild geese arriving last night, who would have seen the autumn at the sea gate?"

If you have attained it, then you are the same as Śākyamuni Buddha; if you have not attained it, then you are the same as Śākyamuni Buddha. Why is this so? Because Śākyamuni Buddha did not attain it himself, and therefore he could not help others to attain it. You all must go forth and seek it yourselves; do not rely on others. If you rely on others, you will lose your own self. If you lose your own self, you will fall into the three evil paths. Therefore, you must each investigate for yourselves. Do not let the days and months pass by in vain. If you can understand this matter right now, then you will know that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are all within your own mind. Do not look for it outside. If you look for it outside, you will be like a dog chasing a stone. Even if you chase it for a hundred years, you will never catch it. Therefore, you must turn back and look within. If you can turn back and look within, then you will see that your own mind is originally the Buddha-mind. There is no need to seek it elsewhere. If you can realize this, then you will be free from birth and death. If you are free from birth and death, then you will be able to benefit yourself and benefit others. This is called attaining the Way. If you attain the Way, then you will be able to manifest various forms according to the capacities of beings, preaching the Dharma to liberate them. This is called great compassion. Great compassion is the root of all Buddhadharmas. Without great compassion, there is no way to attain Buddhahood. Therefore, you must cultivate great compassion. If you cultivate great compassion, then you will naturally give rise to the four immeasurable minds. Once the four immeasurable minds are present, you will naturally give rise to the six paramitas. Once the six paramitas are complete, you will naturally fulfill the ten stages of a Bodhisattva. Once the ten stages are fulfilled, you will naturally attain the three bodies of a Buddha. Once the three bodies are attained, you will naturally manifest the four wisdoms. Once the four wisdoms are manifested, you will naturally turn the great Dharma wheel. Once the great Dharma wheel is turned, you will naturally liberate all sentient beings. This is called the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, you must strive with diligence and not be negligent. If you are negligent, you will fall into the three evil paths. If you fall into the three evil paths, you will suffer immeasurable pain. Therefore, you must be careful. Do not take this lightly. If you take this lightly, you will regret it later. It is said: 'If you do not study the Way in youth, you will regret it when you grow old. You must all exert yourselves to the utmost. Do not let this opportunity pass. If you let it pass, you will repent for a thousand lifetimes. Therefore, I urge you all to practice with single-minded devotion. Do not let your thoughts be distracted. If your thoughts are distracted, you will be unable to attain anything. Therefore, you must concentrate your mind and contemplate the nature of reality. If you contemplate the nature of reality, then you will see that all phenomena are empty and quiescent. If you see that all phenomena are empty and quiescent, then you will naturally be free from all attachments. If you are free from all attachments, then you will naturally give rise to great compassion. If you give rise to great compassion, then you will naturally turn the Dharma wheel and liberate all beings. This is the true meaning of the Buddha's teaching. You must all remember this and apply it in your daily lives. Do not let it remain merely as words. If you let it remain merely as words, you will be like a parrot reciting scriptures—it will be of no benefit to you. Therefore, you must put it into practice. If you put it into practice, then you will truly be a disciple of the Buddha. If you are a disciple of the Buddha, then you will be able to repay the kindness of the Triple Gem. If you can repay the kindness of the Triple Gem, then you will be a person of great merit and virtue. This is what I mean when I say: 'To study the Way is to study the self. To study the self is to forget the self. To forget the self is to be enlightened by all things. To be enlightened by all things is to cast off body and mind, and to leave behind traces in the dust. This is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must all take this to heart. [The Master] then strikes the meditation seat once and descends. All the monks prostrate themselves in gratitude. The Master then leads the assembly out. The record of this event is known as "The Record of the Dharma Talks at Guizong. It is a rare treasure of the Chan school. Those who encounter it should cherish it deeply. Do not treat it lightly. If you treat it lightly, you will miss the great benefit. Therefore, I urge you all to read and recite it often. If you read and recite it often, then you will naturally be transformed and purified. This is the power of the Dharma. You must all believe in this. Do not doubt it. If you doubt it, you will create obstacles for yourself. Therefore, you must believe with all your heart. If you believe with all your heart, then you will be able to attain liberation. This is the true path to enlightenment. I hope you will all take this to heart and put it into practice. Do not let this opportunity pass. If you let it pass, you will repent for a thousand lifetimes. Therefore, I urge you all to strive with diligence and not be negligent. If you are diligent, then you will surely attain the Way. If you attain the Way, then you will be able to benefit yourself and benefit others. This is the ultimate goal of the Buddhist path.
