On behalf of the Patriarch, Xuedou said, "Before you reached Caoxi, I would have given you thirty blows!"

The Master said: "Whether large or small snow beans, whether continuing the mandarin ducks or truncating the cranes, leveling mountains or filling valleys—it does not hinder a skilled hand acting according to the mandate.
Yet, he deserves twenty blows. Why? Because when the waves at Caoxi are like this, countless ordinary people are submerged and lost."
Yangshan held up his staff and pointed to a snow lion, saying, "Is there anyone who can pass through this form?
Yunmen said, "At that moment, I would have pushed it over. Xuedou said, "He only knows how to push it over; he cannot lift it back up."
The Master said: "Yunmen pushed him over; Xuedou helped him up. Even if you can pass through this appearance, you are still not a golden-haired lion.
He then cited Xiangyan’s hanging words: "It is like a man climbing a tree, with his mouth clutching a branch, neither hand grasping a branch nor foot holding onto anything..."
Taozhi was walking beneath a tree when someone suddenly asked him, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
To not answer would have been to disregard the question; to answer, however, would have meant losing his life. At such a moment, what should one do?
There was the Venerable Houtou who said, "I do not ask about having already climbed the tree; please, Master, speak before you have climbed it. Xiangyan laughed heartily.
[The Master] laughed. Xuedou said, "To speak while on the tree is easy; to speak while under the tree is difficult. I, this old monk, am now up in the tree;
bring forth a question!"
The Master said: "Xiangyan exhausted all his spiritual powers, yet he was not spared from a single squeeze of Houtou, whereupon he fell flat on all four corners.
Even if Xuedou possessed vital life-force, he too could not have propped him up."
A monk asked Lu Zu, "What is 'speaking without speaking'? Zu said, "Where is your mouth? The monk said, "I have no mouth.
Zu said, "With what do you eat your rice? The monk was speechless. Xuedou said, "He should have been struck across the back with a staff.
Such fellows cannot close their mouths after they have opened them, nor can they open their mouths after they have closed them."
The Master said: "This monk was so intent on gazing at the white waves that he lost his oar. Had he been a man of true caliber, as soon as [Lu Zu] said, 'Where is your mouth?

he would have overturned the meditation seat. Not only would Lu Zu have raised high his banner of surrender, but he would also have spared himself the embarrassment of being shouted down from behind like a snow bean."

A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? Feng said, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one cannot see the bottom. The monk asked, "And what of those who drink from it?
Feng said, "It does not enter through the mouth. The monk related this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "It cannot enter through the nostrils.
The monk then asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? Zhaozhou said, "Bitter."
The monk asked, "What about one who drinks? Zhaozhou said, "Dead. When Xuefeng heard this being cited, he remarked, "Zhaozhou is an ancient Buddha;
from this point on, he would no longer answer questions. Xuedou said, "Everyone in the assembly says that Xuefeng did not bring up the monk’s question, which is why Zhaozhou was unwilling to engage.
To interpret the matter in such a way deeply wrongs the ancients. Xuedou does not think so; he would have cut it off like chopping through a nail."
Iron. A master of the fundamental division who levels the high by means of the low is difficult to emulate.
The Master said: "Xuefeng’s entire discourse was not realized until he scratched Zhaozhou’s itch;
Zhaozhou could not restrain his amusement and, without realizing it, pricked Xuefeng’s sore spot. Where there is pain, there is itching; where there is itching, there is pain—at once."
This is shifted onto the person of Xuedou. Tell me, has this monk ever seen it even in a dream?
[The Master] cited a monk asking Xitang: "When there is a question and there is an answer, the guest and host are clearly distinguished. But when there is no question and no answer, what then?"
The Hall Master said, "I am afraid it will rot away there. A monk asked Changqing, "When there is a question and an answer, the roles of guest and host are clearly defined;
but what about when there is neither question nor answer? Changqing said, "Everyone they meet says they have retired from office, yet not one person has ever been seen beneath the forest trees.
Xuedou said, "Why not give him his proper portion of fodder?"
The Master said: "Three heads and two faces—this is what people detest. When someone asked Lingyan, "When there is a question and there is an answer, the roles of host and guest are clearly distinct;
but when there is no question and no answer, how is it? He simply replied to him: "How could a turtle ever have escaped from inside a jar?"
Linji addressed the assembly, saying, "In the presence of my former teacher, I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times.
Three times I was struck with sixty blows of the staff, which were like being brushed with a bundle of mugwort. Now I think of giving him another blow; who will step forward to deal it?
At that time, a monk came forth and said, "I, this one, shall deal it. Linji took up his staff and passed it to him. As the monk reached out to receive it, Linji struck him.
Ji (Linji) then struck him. Xuedou said, "Linji’s letting go was perilous; his gathering back was too swift.
The Master said, "Do not speak of 'letting go being perilous' and 'gathering back being too swift. You must know that Linji possesses the mechanism for trapping tigers.
This monk lacked the eye to penetrate the barrier. Had he waited until Linji said, 'I will give you another beating,' who would have been able [to strike]?"
He stepped forward and immediately overturned the meditation seat. This not only cut off the old fellow’s throat, but moreover provided a way for him to manifest himself.
Once, when Qinshan ascended the hall, he raised his fist and then opened it, saying: "When opened, it becomes the palm; the five fingers are distinct."
“Open. He then clenched his fist and said, “Now it is a fist; there is certainly no high or low. Is there anything more to discuss?
A monk stepped forward from the assembly and held up his fist. Xuefeng said, “You are merely a fellow who knows nothing of opening and closing.
Xuedou said, “Xuedou does not think so. He then held up his fist and said, “When clenched, it is a fist; there is high and low. He then opened his hand and said, “Open.”
This is the hand. Without faction and without partiality—tell me: is it better to let go for the sake of others, or is it better to hold fast for the sake of others?
To open is to build a carriage; to grasp is to fit the tracks. If you say that one builds a carriage within the closed door and fits the tracks upon leaving the gate, I know you well.
"You are making your living inside a ghost cave.
The Master said: "Unfolding it is not the palm; grasping it is not the fist. Both ends are completely severed;
a single sword leans against the sky, cold. Now tell me, is there still a way to benefit others? He gave a shout. "The west wind blows across the Wei River; the leaves fall..."
The leaves fill Chang’an.

Muzhou said, “Yesterday someone asked this; I chased him out. The monk said, “Are you perhaps afraid that I am not sincere, Master? Muzhou said, “The staff—”

The Master said: "Xuedou’s critique in this manner deeply wrongs the ancients. I, this mountain monk, say that although Muzhou brought forth the bowl and its contents together, it was simply because he rarely encountered one who could appreciate him."

Huizhao said, "Those who do not enter preserve the community. He continued, "Whether you have realized it or not, you do not enter;
whether you have not realized it or not, you do not enter. The guest replied, "It is not like that at all. Huizhao then struck him and said, "The Rector Kebin has failed in the battle of Dharma.
He shall be fined five strings of cash and must provide a meal for the assembly. On the following day at the time of the midday meal, Huizhao himself struck the gavel and said, "Rector Kebin..."
"If you do not win in battle, you shall not eat your meal; you must leave the monastery immediately. Xuedou said: "Kebin wished to inherit the lineage of Xinghua.
Let us set aside the punishment of money and leaving the monastery for a moment; he must first receive that one blow of the staff before it is complete.
Now I ask you all: since the blow has already been taken, how can he demand it back? Xuedou wishes to settle this matter of injustice; tonight, I shall [provide the verdict]."
Xue Dou struck them all at once with his staff to disperse them.
The Master said: "Xinghua was a general who went out to battle; Kebin was one who held the walls firm and did not fight.

When his strength was exhausted and his skills spent, he could not avoid being forced to surrender like a sheep and hand over the jade璧 (bi). Xue Dou wished to settle this injustice and acted directly to vindicate Kebin’s grievance."
Do you understand? Though one may achieve a moment of glory, one’s two feet are cut off.
A monk asked Changqing, "When many hands sift through gold, who is it that obtains it? Changqing said, "Those with skillful means obtain it."
The monk asked, "Can a student still attain it? Xue Dou said, "It is very far away. On behalf of that monk, Xuedou then gave a shout and further said:
"To those with skillful means, it is given with one hand; to those without skillful means, it is not given even with both hands. Can a student still attain it? Heaven! Heaven!"
The Master said: "Changqing’s 'harmonizing with the bowl' was missed by that monk right before his eyes.

Xuedou could not restrain his impatience and could not help but force the ox's head down to eat the grass. Today, if someone were to ask Lingyan about 'everyone’s hands sifting gold,' [what would he say?]"
"Who is it that attains? He simply said to him: "When the object meets its master, the eye stands upright.
Again he asked, "Does the student attain as well? He replied, "How can one blame this old monk for that?"
Daci raised the topic of great compassion to address the assembly, saying, "I, this mountain monk, do not know how to answer questions; I simply recognize the illness.

At that time, a monk stepped forward, and Daci immediately returned to his quarters. Xuedou said, "In general, when upholding the teachings and the school, one must distinguish between right and wrong."
Furthermore, when Daci recognized the sickness and did not answer the monk’s question, a monk stepped forward and he immediately returned to his quarters.
When Xuedou recognized the sickness and did not answer the monk’s question, if a monk stepped forward, he would strike him across the back with his staff.

When those of various quarters recognized the sickness and did not answer the monk’s question, if a monk stepped forward, they surely possessed some other excellence; had there been even one who dared to move, the Emperor of Great Tang would have had only three [worthy disciples].
The Master said: "Xuedou may indeed cause his fragrance to flow for a thousand ages, yet he has not yet attained utter decisiveness.
According to my own view, one must simply beat him and drag him out. Why? Because the great ocean does not harbor a corpse."
Citing the case of Zhaozhou visiting Huangbo: when Huangbo saw him coming, he immediately closed the door to his quarters.
Zhaozhou shouted from atop the Dharma Hall, "Put out the fire! Put out the fire! Huangbo then came out, seized him, and said, "Speak! Speak!
Zhaozhou replied, "Drawing the bow after the thief has fled. Yunsu said, "Truly a laughable sight; one could laugh for thirty years. Suddenly, a monk asked, "Snow..."

Xuedou says, "What is he laughing at? He is laughing at 'drawing the bow after the thief has fled.'* The Master [Yunmen] says, 'Beating the wooden clappers at the double gates'—Huangbo was overly defensive.

'Biting the arrowhead to break through the pass'—Zhaozhou was habitually adept at seizing the advantage. Although neither harms the other, Xuedou laughs until his own nostrils are split. *This refers to the proverbial phrase "drawing the bow after the thief has fled," implying it is too late for action once the opportunity has passed.

The Master's remark suggests that while Huangbo’s caution is understandable, it is excessive; Zhaozhou’s skillful maneuvering, however, demonstrates a mastery of the situation. Xuedou’s laughter implies that both masters, despite their mutual lack of harm, have been exposed in their respective positions.

Jingqing said, “What source? The monk said, “That source. Jingqing said, “If it is that source, how could it accept a skillful means?
Xuedou said, “To be submerged in dead water—what use is there in that? An attendant asked, “Just now, did you not rebuff him? Jingqing said, “No.”
The attendant said, "He did not remove it. Jingqing said, "No. The attendant asked, "What was your honor’s intention?
Jingqing said, "A single drop of ink; two dragons are formed. Xuedou said, "There is still a bit more room for improvement.
Xuedou did not wish to diminish Jingqing’s majestic brilliance, but rather wanted to meet this monk face-to-face. What is that source? That source, thirty years later...
"I give you thirty blows. The Master said:
"Jingqing’s single drop of ink-water forms dragons in two places; it is enough to overturn the mountain torrents and darken the vast sky with clouds.
Yet Xuedou, wishing to diminish his majestic brilliance, meets this monk in a leisurely and unhurried manner."

"Where does a monk stand in relation to people? At that time, a monk came forward and said, "I dare not arbitrarily create complications.

this staff of mine can kill and can give life; within giving life there is killing, and within killing there is giving life; it may even be both killing and giving life at once."

At the same time, there are instances where killing and giving life do not occur simultaneously. If one employs [this principle] skillfully, there is no dharma—whether mundane or supramundane—that is not fully prepared;

thus, one can observe the exercise of granting and seizing, and the rolling up and unfolding [of phenomena] without obstruction. If one cannot employ it skillfully, it is entirely like binding oneself with a rope that does not even exist.
The Master brought up the story of Yunmen’s three types of sick people as requested by a monk. Yunmen said, "Prostrate yourself.
When the monk rose from his prostration, Yunmen struck him with his staff. The monk stepped back, and Yunmen said, "You are not blind.
He then called the monk forward; as the monk approached, Yunmen said, "You are not deaf. Yunmen asked, "Do you understand? The monk—
The monk said, "I do not understand. Yunmen said, "Are you suffering from dumbness? At this, the monk had an awakening. Xuedou then gave a shout and said, "This blind, deaf, and mute fellow!
Had it not been for Yunmen, he would still be as he is驴年 (a donkey-year) ago. Now, there are some who, when they pick up a mallet or raise a whisk, pay no mind;
they tell him to come forward, yet he does not come. Do you understand? He did not respond. Can the various quarters of the school handle such a person?"
"How can you be like this? If Xuedou were not at his wits' end, what would you—this pack of donkeys—be good for?
With these words, he struck them all at once with his staff and drove them away.
The Master said: "Xuan Sha pointed out three types of symptoms; Yun Men’s one trial is like a nine-fold elixir. How fortunate they were!
Yet, when illness has persisted for long, complications arise. Xuedou was already at his wits' end;
today, this mountain monk cannot help but act as a physician for a dead horse. Raising his whisk, he called to the assembly: "Right here—"
Awakened! With eyes closed, it can be seen; with ears plugged, it can be heard; with the mouth shut, it can be spoken.
Thirty years hence, you shall not be able to say that the Buddha-dharma lacks efficacy.
A monk asked Xiangyan, "What is it when the King asks for *saindhava*? Yan said, "Go ask those over there. Xuedou said, "This is utterly frustrating!
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is it when the King asks for *saindhava*? Zhaozhou bent his body and joined his palms.
Xuedou said, "He asked for salt, but you served him horse-feed."
The Master said: "Xuedou only knew that the King was requesting *santāpa*, but he did not realize that two ancient Buddhas had been missed.
If someone were to ask me, 'What is the King's request for *santāpa*? I would simply tell them:
'Step back! Step back!'"
Gushan raised his staff and addressed the assembly, saying, "If one discusses this matter, it is like a single-bladed sword.
At that time, a monk asked, "I have heard the Master say, 'If one discusses this matter, it is like a single-bladed sword. The Master is a corpse; the student is a corpse.
What, then, is the sword? Gushan said, "Drag out that corpse! The monk responded with an assent and returned beneath his robes and bowl.
He packed his things and departed immediately. That evening, Mount [Gushan] asked the Head Seat, "Is the monk who came to question me still here?
The Head Seat replied, "He left right then. Mount said, "A good twenty blows for him! Xuedou said, "The elders of all quarters all say that Mount Gushan lost one of his eyes;
yet they fail to realize that under a heavy reward, there must be brave men. Nevertheless—"
If one were to examine this closely, it could not avoid being buried all at once.
The Master said: "The hair-cutting blade is held in hand; the entire world is ice and frost. This monk, forgetting his own body, dares to charge toward the snowy edge.
It is a pity he was not cut in two; instead, he draws his bow after the thief has fled. Although Xuedou uses but one hand here—
Raising one hand and making a fist—it is nothing more than a man carrying a corpse.
[The Master] cites Muzhou asking Elder Wuling: "When finished, a hair swallows the vast ocean; only then does one know that the great earth is but a single mote of dust.
[Muzhou asks: "How is this? [Wuling] says: "Whom does the Master ask? [Muzhou] says: "I am asking you, Elder. [Wuling] says: "Why do you not grasp the meaning of my words? [Muzhou] says: "I..."
"Understood? Not understood? Xuedou said, "He has fallen! He has fallen! He added, "This old fellow with his entanglements deserves a clean severing.
Taking up his staff, he said, "Where has he gone?"
The Master said: "Red Hongya strikes White Hongya. Xuedou wishes to cut through this tangle;
it is a fall, indeed a fall!
He cites the case where, while Yangshan was sitting, Dachenfo arrived and stood on one foot, saying, "The twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven..."
It is thus. The Sixth Patriarch of the Tang land was also thus. The Master was also thus. So-and-so was also thus.
On the meditation seat beneath the mountain, four strokes of the rattan were struck. Xuedou said: "The rattan has not yet reached breaking; for what reason did he strike only four times?
One must be a man who can cut through nails and sever iron before this will suffice. Later, Dachen Fo arrived at Huoshan and himself...
Yunmen said, "Four willow branches beneath Cloud-Gathering Peak; the Great Zen Buddha of the world comes to inquire.
Shanshan said, "Strike the bell! And Chan immediately ran off. Xuedou said, "This fellow acted upon seeing the signs; yet, alas, he has a head but no tail."
The Master said, "Little Śākyamuni could not hold fast the secure barrier, causing this fellow to carry four blows from the rattan cane everywhere, parading them about.
Had it not been for Huo Shan, he would have nearly broken into Cai Zhou.
Xuedou said, "Before the rattan canes were even broken, why did he only strike him four times? What does he know of good and evil?"
To cite Xuansha and Tianlong: While entering the mountains, they encountered a tiger. Long said, "The tiger is ahead. Sha said, "It is you.
Xuedou said, "If you wish to be a teacher for humans and devas, that which is right before you is truly a tiger."
The Master said: "Tianlong is the tiger; Xuansha is you. Great as Xuedou may be, he must act differently to establish his own eye before he can serve as a teacher to gods and men."
It is said that beneath Nanquan there was a hut master. A traveling monk passed by and said to him, "The Master Nanquan has recently appeared in the world;
why do you not go to pay him homage? The master replied, "Not only Nanquan—even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world, I still could not go.
When Nanquan heard of this, he ordered Zhaozhou to go see him. Upon seeing the master, Zhaozhou immediately prostrated himself. The master—
Regardless, the monk went from west to east; the Master still did not acknowledge him. The monk then went from east to west; the Master still did not acknowledge him.
The monk said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated," pulled down the curtain, and departed. Upon returning, he related this to Nanquan. Nanquan said:
"One who has always harbored doubts is this fellow. Xuedou said, "Big and little Nanquan and Zhaozhou have been seen through by this board-carrying fellow.
The Master said, "Forged from solid steel, cast from raw iron. Xuedou said, "Big and little Nanquan and Zhaozhou."
He was thoroughly exposed by this fellow carrying a wooden board on his back. He only knew that opening one's mouth is easy, yet he failed to realize how long his own tongue is.
I dare say that even the masters of the world could not withstand a single glance from this old man.
A monk asked Fengxue: "When speech and silence involve transcendence and subtlety, how can one pass through without transgression? Fengxue said:
"I always remember that in the third month of Jiangnan, where the partridges cry, the hundred flowers are fragrant. Xuedou said: "Once someone asked Xuedou [the same question]."
He said to him: "To split open the belly and gouge out the heart—how so? He replied: "To fan the fire with the wind is a distinct tradition;
to harm the turtle while sparing the tortoise must surely have its master."
The Master said: "Not involving departure or subtlety, completely transcending speech and silence. Where the partridge cries, it causes people to remember;
rending the belly and gouging out the heart, one mechanism is revealed. This is a truly extraordinary piece of good news from the Real Man. Do you see these two elders?
They take up the unperforated flute of Shaolin and blow it deep into the night across the waters of the Muzitan."
[The Master] raised the cases of Yantou, Yunfeng, and Qingshan. When they arrived at Deshan, Qingshan asked, "Tianhuang spoke thus;
Longtan spoke thus. I wonder, how would Deshan speak? Deshan said, "Try citing what Tianhuang and Longtan said and see.
As Qingshan hesitated, Deshan struck him. After being struck, Qingshan went to the Hall of Longevity and said, "It is so, it is so."
"Beating me so severely! Yan said, "If you act like this, you shall not be able to say later that you have seen Deshan.
Xuedou said, "All you Zen adepts, Qingshan’s question was truly extraordinary; yet, alas, he had the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake.
Try reciting the case of Tianhuang and Longtan for yourselves: [Longtan] struck his sitting cloth, and [Tianhuang] said, 'A great man plucks the tiger's whiskers.'"
This is one's own fundamental duty. Since he was unable to do so, Deshan ordered that half be practiced;
had the order been carried out in its entirety, Xuefeng and Yantou would both have been men of the Nirvana Hall.
The Master said: "When three people walk together, there is bound to be one who possesses wisdom. Since Qinshan was unable to speak, did Xuefeng and Yantou manage to speak?
Setting aside for a moment whether they spoke or not, Xuedou said: "Deshan’s command has been carried out only halfway.
If the command had been fully executed, Xuefeng and Yantou would both be men in the Hall of Nirvana. It is just like this:
Xuedou: "Is he still able to avoid it? [He] cites a monk asking Zhimen:
"What is the essence of prajñā? Zhimen said: "An oyster containing the bright moon. The monk asked: "What is the function of prajñā?
Zhimen said: "A rabbit conceiving a fetus. Xuedou said: "Not only does he hold fast to the world,"
This will surely bring peace and stability to the state and the family. If you can thoroughly investigate and deliberate upon this, you may then request to stride alone through the crimson heavens.
The Master said: "The oyster contains the bright moon; the rabbit carries a fetus in its womb. From where did you receive this news?
To hold fast to the world and establish peace for the state—believe only half of that.
Regarding the case of Wujou: when the two senior monks Xuanshao arrived, Wujou asked, "You two Chan masters, where have you recently come from?
The monks replied, "Jiangxi. Wujou struck him. The monk said, "I have long heard that the Master possesses such a vital pivot.
Wujou said, "Since you do not understand, the second one, come forward. As the monk hesitated, Wujou struck him again, saying, "In the same pit, there is no different soil."
"Go to the hall," Xuedou said. "The eyes of a true master must reach such a state: like a golden-winged garuḍa cleaving the sea, it goes straight for the dragon to swallow it.
There are a certain sort of fellows whose eyes cannot distinguish east from west, who do not even know when their staff is upside down;
they do nothing but talk of 'illumination and function occurring simultaneously' and 'seizing both person and environment.'"
The Master said: "Wujou sat occupying the main hall; his true command was being exercised. That monk came from afar seeking his reputation and was destined to receive a blow of the staff.
If one were a seasoned veteran of the battle, where would there be a Wujou? Furthermore, if you have not yet understood..."
Look at Xuedou’s entanglement.
A monk took his leave of Da-sui. Da-sui asked, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to Mount Emei to pay homage to Samantabhadra.
Da-sui held up his whisk and said, "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are both right here. The monk drew a circle and threw it away.
Behind the scenes, Sui said: "The attendant brought a bowl of tea and gave it to that monk. Yunmen added: "In India they cut off heads and arms;
here, take it yourself and go out. Xuedou said: "It is the blade that kills and the sword that gives life; those with discerning eyes must distinguish it."
The Master said, "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are both right here. Because of his great compassion, Dàsuí engaged in this talk that descended to the common level.
The monk drew a circle, threw it behind him, and shouted, "Tsk! You dead shrimp! Suí said:
The attendant brought a bowl of tea for the monk who had been given the slip of paper. What kind of mental activity was this? Yunmen said instead:
"In India they cut off heads and arms; here, go out and receive it yourself. This is like adding frost to snow. Xuedou said:
"The sword that kills and the sword that gives life—no expert can discern them."
Xuefeng called out to a monk, saying, "I have heard it said that you, Venerable One, once came as a celestial messenger—is this true?
The monk replied, "I dare not say so. Xuefeng asked, "How could you come in such a manner? The monk said, "Admiring your virtue and wisdom, how could I have feared the mountain passes?
Xuefeng said, "You are still drunk; get out! The monk then departed. Xuefeng then called out, "Venerable One! The monk turned his head back, and Xuefeng said, "What is this?"
[The Master] said, "What? The monk also said, "What is it? Feng said, "This lacquer bucket. The monk was speechless.
Feng then looked back at Jingqing and said, "A fine monk indeed, who has entered right into a lacquer bucket. Jingqing said, "Does the Master not settle the case according to the facts?
Feng said, "That is what I usually use. But suppose someone suddenly calls out, 'What is this? and is caught [in the trap]."
"The other fellow is a lacquer bucket. "Furthermore, how is it? Qing said, "What kind of principle is that? Feng said, "I reach him in this way;
you then say, 'Based on the facts, the case is closed. He reaches me in that way; you then say, 'What kind of principle is that?
At one and the same time, there is therein attainment and non-attainment. Qing said, "Have you not seen it said? *Tí* (Essence)..."
Ghee is the supreme flavor, prized by the world; yet for those who encounter it, it turns into poison. Xuedou said: "Observe how this father and son meet, their words and spirit in perfect accord.
Those who understand this say that even if one were to grind one's bones to powder and shatter one's body to pieces, this debt of gratitude could never be repaid."

Those who do not understand say that it elevates the high and suppresses the low, or that it strikes terror into people when they face danger; they treat poison as nectar. This has been a mirror for reflection for a thousand years.
Do you understand? You lacquer bucket!
The Master said: "This monk came specifically as a celestial messenger, yet he has, for no reason, bumped into a lacquer bucket.
Xuefeng and Jingqing were long renowned for their skillful hands, yet they could not save him. This poisonous medicine and ambrosial nectar serve as a mirror for a thousand years."
"Not one who knows the heart; in vain do they speak of the 'cold of the year'.
[The Master] raised a case where a monk asked Damei, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Damei said, "There is no meaning in his coming from the West.
The monk brought this up to Yanguan, who said, "One coffin, two dead men. When Xuansha heard this being cited, he said, "Yanguan..."
The official is a master of the Way. Xuedou said, "Even three are acceptable.
The Master said, "It is like a mantis trying to catch a cicada.
He then cited Yunmen’s question to a monk from Silla: "Where are you from? The monk replied, "I am from Silla. Yunmen asked, "What..."
Yunmen said, "Crossing the sea. The monk said, "The grass-thief has been utterly defeated. Yunmen said, "Why is he in my hands? The monk said, "Exactly so.
Yunmen said, "He may leap as much as he pleases. Xuedou said, "Old man Yunmen, you have the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake.
Why did you let this monk go? 'Why is he in my hands? Exactly so'—at that point, he should have struck him across the back!"
The Master said: "This monk has crossed the sea to come here; he has fallen right into Yunmen’s hands.
Xuedou pushes the waves and assists the current—this may be called 'a small emergence meeting a great encounter.'"
Beichan asked a monk: "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "Huangzhou. Beichan asked, "Where were you during the summer retreat?
The monk said, "Zifu. Beichan asked, "With what do you provide for that merit? The monk said, "A double case. Beichan said, "How can it be when it is in my hands?
The monk said, "If it is in your hands, then take it. Beichan struck him. This monk was dissatisfied and followed after him.
He drove him out. Xuedou said, "Remarkable! He truly possesses a composition that surpasses his teacher. Do you know this monk? He only knows how to look ahead;
he cannot look behind. Had he been in Xuedou’s hands, even if the staff were broken, I would not have let him go."
The Master said: "If you do not do it once, do not stop at two. To strike a person, one must have an iron fist. He cited Muzhou’s address to the assembly:
"I saw Baizhang; he did not know good from bad. Just as the great assembly had gathered, he struck them all at once with his staff and scattered them.
He then called out to the assembly, and when they turned their heads, Baizhang asked, 'What is this? What is there?"
At the place where they were conversing, when the assembly had just gathered, Master Huangbo struck them all at once with his staff.
He then called out to the assembly; as the crowd turned their heads, Huangbo said, "The moon is like a drawn bow; light rain and much wind—it is still somewhat lacking.
Xuedou said, "What do you mean by 'still somewhat lacking'? It is simply not yet there. According to Xuedou, when the assembly had gathered...

At that moment, he struck it down and stopped. There may be someone with an unperforated iron hammer who exerts their utmost strength for the sake of the assembly, being truly capable of bearing the burden and encompassing both past and present, holding fast over heaven and earth. Suddenly, picking up his staff, he said: "I let this one move pass."
The Master said: "These three sections are distinct; they are subsumed under the preceding category.
He cited the case where Xuansha saw Gushan approaching and drew a circle. Gushan said, "No one can get out of this."
Sandow said, "I know full well that you are making your living in the wombs of donkeys and horses.
Shan said, "And what about you, Master? Sandow said, "No one can get out of this. Shan said, "Master, you can say such things;
why can't I? Sandow said, "I can, but you cannot. Xuedou said, "He only knows how to greedily gaze at it."
White waves. He did not know he had lost his oar.
The Master said: "If you can speak it, you cannot get out of this; if you cannot speak it, you cannot get out of this."
Gazing greedily at the white waves, he lost his oar. This is idle talk.
[The Master] cites Nanquan’s address to the assembly: "Wang Laoshi is selling himself; is there anyone who will buy?
A monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "I will buy him. Nanquan said, "Neither as something expensive nor as something cheap—how do you buy him? The monk was speechless.
Yuwang said, "The Master belongs to me. Heshan asked, "What kind of principle is that? Zhaozhou said, "Next year I will make a cloth robe for the Master.
Xuedou said, "Although these masters compete to buy it up, they nonetheless do not understand how to yield the strategic point.
But tell me, would Nanquan have approved? Xuedou is also about to offer a price."
This causes Nanquan to have no door for advancing and no path for retreating. Neither acting noble nor acting base—how can you buy him?
No other place can accommodate the Master.
The Master said: "Nanquan is skilled at selling; Xuedou is skilled at buying. Without a broker or guarantor, it remains merely a talk of credit.
Neither making it expensive nor making it cheap, he meets things as they arise and responds to conditions. Riding upon skillful means, he flows forth to the ends of the earth—how pitiable!"
"It would be better to simply turn [the wheel] within the house.
*Tut!* He picked up a piece of *jūyū* (evodia) and a notched bamboo stick, ascended the hall, and said: "Is there anyone who can drive a stake into empty space?"
At that time, the Elder Lingxu stepped forward and said, "Empty space is the stake. Nanquan then struck him. Lingxu said, "Do not strike me by mistake.
Nanquan then desisted. Xuedou said, "If you want this story to spread far and wide, you must have struck him and driven him out immediately."
The Master said: "Zuyu drives a stake into the air; Lingxu suffers a stake driven into barren ground.

Xuedou does not care that "exhausting the law leaves no subjects," he only desires that the story endure for a thousand ages. Examining this from start to finish, they are all nothing but a pack of hollow-boasting braggarts.
Once, while Jiashan and Dingshan were traveling together and engaged in conversation, Dingshan said, "If there is no Buddha within birth and death, then there is no birth and death.
Jiashan said, "If there is a Buddha within birth and death, then one does not become deluded by birth and death. They disagreed with one another and went together to visit Damei.
Having related their previous discussion in detail, Damei said, "One is intimate; the other is distant. Jiashan asked, "Which one is intimate?"
"Which one is distant? Jia said, "Go for now and come back tomorrow. When Jia arrived the following day and asked again, "I wonder which one is intimate?
Mei said, "The intimate does not ask; the questioner is not intimate. After Jia Shan took up residence [elsewhere], he said, "At that time, while I was at Dàméi, I lost an eye.
Xuědòu said, "In the end, Jia Shan did not know he had gained an eye."

Eyes! Great Master Damei, had you heard this case cited at that time and struck them both down with a single blow of your staff, you would have not only cut through the entanglements of these two men, but would also have been a true patriarch of the world.

The Master said: "Jiashan lost one of his eyes; it was only after he took up residence that he came to know this. Xuedou cuts through the entanglements and establishes himself as a patriarch of the world.
Nevertheless, General Li had a fine reputation; even if he did not receive a fief, it was still a matter of no small consequence."
A monk asked Baofu, "Throughout his life, what words or phrases did Xuefeng have that could be compared to 'the wild goat hanging from its horns'?
Baofu said, "I cannot fail to be Xuefeng’s disciple. Xuedou remarked, "Among fifteen hundred monks, Baofu was the one who stood out."
The Master said: "To be a disciple of Xuefeng is not impossible; yet to see the 'wild goat hanging from its horns'—that would take sixty kalpas over three lifetimes.

He cited a monk who asked Changqing, "What is it like before the wild goat has hung from its horns? Changqing said, "A fellow of the weeds. The monk said: [The Master continued: "A fellow of the weeds."
"After the horn has been hung, what then? Changqing said, "He makes a confused clamor. The monk asked, "Ultimately, how is it?

Changqing said, "The business of the donkey has not yet gone; the business of the horse has arrived. Xuedou said, "I would rather have my body shattered into fine dust than ever blind the eyes of a sentient being.
Changqing was off by a hair's breadth. He added, "A man of the same sort—even if the *rāṅga* antelope had not yet hung its horn..."
"It is like gazing ten thousand *li* toward one's hometown.
The Master said, "If Changqing answers a question in such a manner, he will blind the eyes of all people under heaven. Xuedou said:
In the end, he never blinds the eyes of a single sentient being. Ten thousand *li* away, one gazes toward the home district. A monk asked Baling:
"Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different? Baling said: "When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree;

when the duck is cold, it goes down into the water. A monk asked Muzhou: "Are the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings the same or different? Muzhou said: "The green mountains..."
Green mountains; white clouds are simply white clouds. Xuedou said: "The question is one way, and the answer is likewise similar.
Within this, there is benefiting others and benefiting oneself, deceiving others and deceiving oneself. If you can examine it with clarity, you will surely be foremost in understanding emptiness."
The Master said: "When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree; when the duck is cold, it enters the water. The green mountains are towering; the white clouds are vast and serene.
Wherein lie the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings? If one examines this with clarity, whether there is gain or loss, it does not depart from the marketplace."
Jue Zhaozhou addressed the assembly, saying, "Tonight I shall answer questions. Anyone who can ask a question, come forward! At that time, a monk stepped forth.
Zhaozhou said, "I intended to throw a brick to draw out a jade; instead, I have drawn out a mere brick.
Fayan subsequently raised this case and asked Jue Tiezui, "What was the meaning of the former master? Jue replied, "It is like the state appointing a general. He then asked, "In what way?"
"He can go. At that time, someone came forward and said, "I, [Name], can go. [Fayan] must have said, "You cannot go. Fayan said, "I understand.
Xuedou said, "A person of keen intelligence; upon hearing this mention, they immediately know where it lands. Nevertheless, even so..."
Letting go of the realization of "Iron Beak. Now, the words of a true master are never uttered in vain; one who comes forth must surely be a master of the craft.
Why is this? It is like throwing a brick to draw out a tile. All you Zen adepts, do you wish to recognize Zhaozhou? No one has recognized his past labors on the battlefield.
"If one were to re-examine his epoch-making achievements," the Master said, "Jue Tiezui’s fame resounded throughout the universe; yet, when pressed, he immediately emitted the stench of excrement.

When someone asked about "throwing a brick to draw out a tile," [the Master] said, "It was like the state appointing a general. At that time, if Fayan had been able to bring forth the original [principle],...
"Distributing fodder—how could it stop at 'ten thousand miles of pure breeze'? Xuedou said, "A person of keen intelligence would know the point of landing with a single stroke;
how could they be fit for conversation? Nevertheless, even so, I let Jue Tiezui off the hook; it is thanks to these words."
Danyuan took his leave of National Teacher Huairang and returned to visit Mazu. He drew a circle on the ground, spread out his sitting mat, and prostrated.
Mazu said, "You wish to become a Buddha, do you not? Danyuan replied, "I do not know how to rub my eyes. Mazu said, "I am not as good as you.
Xuedou said, "Though a fierce tiger does not devour its own offspring, it cannot be denied that the words he spoke were not generous. All [the masters] said this.
"Do you people know Danyuan? He was simply a fellow who hid his body while exposing his shadow.
The Master said, "When Danyuan returned home for a visit, he offered a 'Hu-bing' (a sesame cake). Mazu licked his calf; he could not help himself.
Xuedou said, "Even a fierce tiger does not eat its own offspring, yet how can one blame him for the lack of abundance in his words? When examined closely," [the truth is revealed].
This precisely steps upon the shadow of Danyuan.
It recalls how Guishan asked Yangshan, "Where have you come from? Yang replied, "From the fields. Guishan asked, "How many people are there in the fields?
Yang stuck his hoe into the ground and stood with his hands folded behind his back. Guishan said, "There are many people on South Mountain mowing thatch. Yang then pulled out his hoe.
He then departed. Xuansha said, "If I had seen him at that time, I would have kicked over his spade. Jingqing said, "What can you do about the boat? Break the scoop!
A monk asked Mingzhao, "The ancients' intent lay in the place where the spade was stuck, or in the place where the hands were folded.
Mingzhao called out, "Somadatta! The monk responded, "Yes? Mingzhao said, "Have you ever dreamed of Yangshan? Xuedou said, "The various quarters..."
Everyone says that the story of planting the spade is extraordinary, yet it is very much like following the heterodox and pursuing evil.
According to Xuedou’s insight, when Yangshan was questioned by Guishan, he was so thoroughly bound by his own straw ropes that he was ten parts closer to death.
The Master said: "In the dialogue between master and disciple at Mt. Gui and Yangshan, there is nothing at all obscure or contradictory.
It was Xuefeng who, like Xuansha, raised waves where there was no wind. Jingqing said: "When the boat cannot be saved, break the scoop!
When a single wave stirs, ten thousand follow. This was not Mingzhao peeling off the skin; otherwise, they would all have died under the spade. (Xue)
Dongyun said: "Yangshan, having been questioned by Guishan, was so thoroughly bound by his own cords that he was dead in every respect.
'Tsk! To use oneself as an obstacle for others.'"
Xuan Sha asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "Ruigan. Xuan Sha asked, "What words or phrases did Ruigan speak?

The monk said, "In one way, it is all a matter of playing with the spirit; how truly strange!
The monk said, "Why not simply remain dwelling within that state? The monk said, "He has already passed away. The monk said, "Can he still be made to respond now?
The monk was speechless. Xuedou said, "Alas! Alas!"
The Master said: "This monk merely picks up echoes and receives empty air; he has heard it on the road and repeated it from hearsay.

It is none of your business, *ācārya*. Xuedou said, "He can distinguish and discern; he can kill and give life."
"If a person can discern this, they may roam freely throughout the world.
The Master said, "Xuefeng asked well; Fuchuan answered well. This monk has the merit of being a swift and capable traveler;
he deserves twenty blows of the staff. Do you understand this thoroughly? Had it not been for Yang Deyi, who would have recognized Ma Xiangru?"
Deshan Yuanming raised his finger to instruct the assembly, saying: "Whenever there was a question or answer, he would simply point with one finger.
When it was cold, 'the whole sky and the whole earth were cold. Xuedou said: 'Where did you see Old Jueyi? When it was hot, 'the whole sky and the whole earth were hot.'"
Yun Dou said: "Do not mistake the markings on the scale of a balance. From the myriad phenomena of the forested world down to the solitary peril;
from the great earth, mountains, and rivers up to the absolute precipice—where can one find even a single finger’s worth of Zen?"
The Master said: "Yuanying borrows a hand to perform a fist; Xuedou chases the wind and pursues lightning.

[Guo] suddenly asked: "If Yunmen says, 'A single phrase that fits the head is a donkey-tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas,' how can one avoid this fault?

The Master said: "One who does not crave the taste of fragrant bait may truly be called a dragon in a azure pool. Xuedou said: "Do not say that because the water is cold the fish will not eat;
now he has caught a full boat and returns home. What use have a lame tortoise or a blind turtle?"

It is encircled by successive layers of fragrant seas, its foundation extending from the base of the mountain to the limits of the Golden Wheel.
The *cakra* pinnacle reaches up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; it has fifty-two tiers of gradations and one hundred ten railings.
Ten voids are filled with pervasive jeweled nets, from which clouds of all manner of offering implements flow forth.
The Bodhi tree blooms with flowers of wisdom, and gardens and ponds emerge as treasuries of merit. The Buddha’s bodily radiance eclipses the sun and moon, while the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas...
The assembly was incalculable, yet the Lords of the World called it "Sublime Array. Each one gathered like clouds in the Hall of Universal Light;

though divided into seven locations and nine assemblies, in truth they did not depart from the Bodhimanda. This original teacher of mine, Vairocana, is surely no different from the Buddhas of the ten directions.
As I contemplate the various World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, the bodies and lands they manifest are entirely equal. And...
Within the net of lands of all the World-Honored Ones, there shall emerge bhikṣus who produce these scriptural volumes.

Their skillful means are universally supreme, and the Buddha-works they perform are no different [from those of the Buddhas]. The Buddhas are equal, their lands are equal, and their assemblies are equal;
so too are their compassionate wisdom, practices, and vows. Such an unsurpassed stūpa is entirely the Dharma-body King Vairocana; the Dharma-body of Vairocana enters [it].

My nature is identical to the nature of Vairocana. I vow that the clouds of all my bodies shall be endowed with an ocean of immeasurable eloquence, and throughout the bounds of the future, they shall praise this stupa no differently than I do now.
These words of mine are quiescent in their characteristics; they resonate in perfect accord with the Tathāgata-mind of all Buddhas. Whether one sees, hears, or rejoices in this, may each awaken.
Attaining the prediction of the Way through their own nature.
Praise for the Dharma-Flower Stupa:
A man of the Way sat in summer retreat at Lotus Peak; rising at dawn, he painted the Lotus Stupa, deeply entering the wondrous threefold [teachings] of the Lotus Sutra.
In a state of profound clarity, he immediately attained *dhāraṇī*. From all eighty-four thousand pores of his body, light was emitted, illuminating heaven and earth.
This very body is the stūpa, and the stūpa is the sūtra; it is free from names and forms, transcending subject and object.

All Buddhas of the ten directions rejoiced, and with one voice they praised him, saying, "Excellent! One should know that throughout the entire career of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, during this single dispensation...

In three hundred assemblies, he taught the Dharma, opening the provisional to reveal the real and demonstrating the essential truth. This sutra alone is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.

At that time, amidst the great assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, I once entrusted this sutra to you. Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, riding upon your original vow, you have been born into the final age of the five turbidities;
donning the armor of diligence with your whole being, you shall sustain and nurture it with a firm resolve for the rest of your life.
To extinguish the prison of absurdity, folly, and darkness, this blazing banner of radiant light is raised;

to open wide the gateway of one’s own spiritual powers and to manifest the ocean of the Buddhas’ knowledge and vision. Even before a single stroke had yet been formed, this stupa already filled the entire realm.
The ancient Buddhas within the stupa and the Buddhas of the present do not emerge from the earth, but appear from the mind. This is why the brush was drawn.

The lines of ink are applied; their arrangement is both pervasive and perfectly integrated, entirely without obstruction. The tiers of the wheel-ornaments rise most loftily; jeweled nets and clouds of incense pervade everywhere.
Celestial flowers fall in profusion, fresh and beautiful; the pure and resonant sound of Dharma vibrates like golden bells.
Whether heard or seen, one awakens to primordial wisdom—this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. I address you, O devas, nāgas, and spirits: in...
In every place, he provides protection and defense, so that this precious stupa may remain firm through vast kalpas, forever bringing benefit to all living beings.
This stupa of the Lotus Sutra is the master of the Dharma-treasury;
I praise this treasury of the Lotus Sutra as being profound, solid, and far-reaching, revealing it for others to awaken to and enter, encompassing the entire great trichiliocosm.
Excellent, O Superior One! With your wondrous wisdom of non-action, you have encompassed all within a single hair-tip and conjured this great jeweled stupa.
It is so high and vast that it reaches the Brahma world; it extends through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, neither interrupted nor extinguished, neither worn away nor collapsed.
Furthermore, within every thought-moment, one shall initiate the various deeds of the Buddhas; whether by seeing them or making offerings, one will swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood.
You should know that this precious stupa is entirely the Puṇḍarīka; it reveals the provisional to manifest the ultimate, thereby accomplishing all meanings.
This is called the king among sūtras; it is the foremost within the stūpa. The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the present always abide therein.
The lattices of their lands reflect one another, and all the emanation Buddhas assemble there simultaneously. It is both the speaker and that which is spoken.

The characteristics of words are quiescent; there is neither grasping nor realization. To be in perfect union with the mind of all Buddhas—those who can accord with this mind attain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
For your sake, I have praised this stūpa by reciting these sublime verses through the power of your diligence.

This stirs my mind toward indolence; thus I know this superior person is my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). I observe the lands of the ten directions, and there is nowhere this sutra is not present.
In the final age of the Buddhas' Dharma, there is no one who does not inscribe it upon these stupas. There are also those who offer praises to the stupas.
It shall not differ from my own; because of abiding securely in these four dharmas, one immediately possesses the path of Samantabhadra. I prostrate to Śākyamuni;
may he bear witness to my words thus spoken.
Wang Pengmei’s Engraved Copy of the Eulogy on King Aśoka’s Stūpa:
Regarding King Aśoka, he possessed the ground of great causes. In the past, as a young child, he gathered sand while playing; by chance, the Buddha arrived.
In his joyful veneration, he lacked the means to express his sincerity; he offered sand as *maṇḍaka* (flour-cakes), and the Buddha praised him, saying, "Excellent!

He then bestowed upon him a prophecy: "In a future life, you shall attain the rank of a Cakravartin King of Iron Wheels. Fully endowed with the ten wholesome paths of action, the myriad regions shall submit to your rule. Though you dwell in the world,"
And they shall enjoy celestial blessings. They shall construct eighty-four thousand precious stupas for me and enshrine my relics within them, extensively benefiting humans and devas.
Adorned and magnificently decorated, they shall be established day and night without ceasing, employing spirits and deities to distribute them throughout the world after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

The result accorded with past conditions; whatever was to be done occurred exactly so. At that time, there was a venerable one named Yaśas, who emitted light from his five fingers, scattering like flying arrows.
Wherever the light reached, the stupa followed accordingly, as a rain of various flowers fell in profusion.
Guarded by devas and nāgas, this is the land of China, east of Kuaiji. It is here that the śarīra rests; it is called Mount Mò.
Through the mutual resonance of the Way, it is neither near nor far, yet it appeared through Liu Sahe. Its pinnacle consists of five tiers.
The corner eaves rise on all four sides; it is four chi in height and half that in width. Precious bells hang within, while sacred images are displayed without.

Auspicious colors and auspicious light shimmer and penetrate with crystalline clarity. From the Jin through the Liang, across the Chen and the Tang, and down to the Wu, Yue, and Southern Song dynasties.

Miraculous manifestations appeared one after another. Reaching our Great Yuan Dynasty, when the empire was unified under a single system of chariots and books, the precious stupa was subsequently welcomed into the capital.

Grand assemblies were held in succession to pray for the blessing of the state; its light illuminated the imperial court, its brilliance eclipsing the sight of all present, as the hundred officials presented their congratulations.

The Emperor’s countenance was filled with great joy; he prostrated himself and circumambulated [the remains] three times, his devotion equaling that of one who would scatter his hair upon the ground. He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddha’s compassion regards all equally, and his methods for gathering and transforming beings are most skillful.
How could we allow him to remain long detained? You should escort him back to Ningbo to lay him to rest, so that his legacy may endure for ten thousand generations."
To bring peace and prosperity to my people. Forty years later, Wang of Jinhua exhausted his skills and applied himself with vigor to carve and engrave this image for its distribution.
From east to west, from south to north, may it be honored according to the Dharma; through these immeasurable merits, I contemplate the ten directions.
The Buddha-body is but one, yet these relics manifest universally throughout all atoms. Within each and every atom, the worlds of the ten directions are contained.

The Buddha-body and its relics are neither present nor absent; why do they conceal themselves and then appear? Why are they born and then extinguished? When one contemplates with a single thought, all is transparently clear.
"Empty flowers and the moon in water—thus I speak; it is true and not false. I bow my head to the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni.
To Mañjuśrī, the Great Being, great wisdom is beyond names. True emptiness leaves no trace; both ordinary and sage are forgotten. Essence and function are both quiescent. His eyes flash..."
A flash of lightning! His hair flows like clouds of emerald green. Grasping a sharp sword, he confronts the Elder Gautama; brandishing a *cintāmaṇi*, he faces Vimalakīrti.
Entering the mud and entering the water, his Way transcends ordinary sentiment. Neither silent nor speaking, his meaning reaches its ultimate limit.

Concealing his mechanism in the dark, he discerns the mark within the light. Walls, fences, tiles, and rubble shake the earth and emit radiance. The scabby dog and the mud-pig display their full majesty.
He whirled [the text] back;
his lacquered eyes were piercingly bright, and his deep blue hair hung down in long strands. Holding a scroll, he stood out alone, his solitary wind chilling and majestic.

He rebuked the various disciples who had shattered the Great Way, and by propagating correct wisdom, he swept away all doubts. Whether it was Mañjuśrī or not Mañjuśrī, the clouds parted to reveal the azure sky.
Emerging from the Dharma-realm and entering the Dharma-realm, the full moon hangs over the earth; dragons and snakes are intermingled, and ordinary beings dwell together with sages.
Clad in grass, he moves with a shuffling gait—the teacher of the seven Buddhas.
I am the true Mañjuśrī; he cannot be portrayed or described. There is no such thing as Mañjuśrī; I take the mistaken for the correct.
The golden-maned lion unleashes its full majesty, casually snapping off the horn of the auspicious qilin.
The Great Being Samantabhadra is the source of the school of "hearing with the mind" and the progenitor of the ocean of vows.

With disheveled hair and clad in coarse grass garments, though he has come from the kingdom of Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, he dwells inseparable from the body of Vairocana Buddha; his entire being is eye.
There is no tracing of its traces or origins; seeing the essence as entirely true, how can it be caught or grasped? Where the Elephant King turns, a hundred flowers bloom red;
in every land and every atom of dust, we behold one another face-to-face.

Shattering a single atom, a great scripture emerges; though the strokes and characters have not yet taken form, their patterns are already manifest. Principle follows the transformations of phenomena as the sun shines and heaven looks down;
when phenomena attain the fusion of principle, they revolve like pearls and turn like jade. Its essence pervades the realms of all sands, yet even the Universal Eye remains deluded.
The mind penetrates the ten directions, beyond the discrimination of Mañjuśrī; one surely knows that the trampling of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure.
It is only fitting, therefore, that such a being should blend water with mud and leave its head disheveled and face begrimed.

The Layman Vimalakīrti struck down the biased and disparaged the narrow gates of the Lesser Vehicle, extolling the Great and praising the principles of the Perfect Teaching. By manifesting illness in the city of Vaiśālī, he stirred the five regions of India into a state of tumultuous agitation.
He swallowed the vast ocean within a single hair and severed the Land of Wonderful Joy like a potter’s wheel; he contained Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed. There was...
Liberation is called the inconceivable. How many know it when leaning over toward Mañjuśrī? Stretching out the legs is right within drawing them back;
the skeletal frame is rugged and prominent, the old heart is vast and empty. Mañjuśrī does not come, and there is no skill whatsoever.
To call this the response-body of Golden Grain is merely striking the air to seek a sound. It is laughable that those at the assembly on Vulture Peak each anticipated the wind before it blew.
My courage fails me;
this entire body is utterly helpless. Again, you carry Miaoxi into the Sahā world.
Beyond repaying people with a single silence, is there anything further that can sever the myriad stimuli?
Vimalakīrti remained silent for a moment; the Gate of Non-duality opened. He held the great trichiliocosm in his hand, moving it back and forth upon the tip of a single hair.

Through the power of diligent cultivation of hearing and the practice of hearing, the Great Being Avalokiteśvara attained the inconceivable Vajra Samādhi, wherein the six sense faculties function interchangeably in perfect fullness.
Pervasive! Excellent is this supernatural power, this unique dharma. A single dharma is fully endowed with all dharmas; it encompasses the oceans of lands without mutual obstruction.
Like the moon moving through space, it is reflected in water; wave after wave appears instantaneously, yet these are not its true nature.

One who attains clear realization here penetrates the boundless; looking back at one's own nature, all is found to be equal. Since phenomena and self are fundamentally non-dual, one is then able to be universal.
Operate with a mind of compassion. The wisdom of a single thought-moment enters immeasurable eons; the wisdom of immeasurable eons enters a single thought-moment.
The past does not go forth, the future does not come; the present is suchness, yet it abides nowhere. A single body pervades the worlds of the ten directions; myriad forms interact without exertion.
The worlds of the ten directions again enter a single body; quiescent, profound, and eternally true, it is free from clamor and confusion.
That which is pleasure, that which is suffering, and that which is neither suffering nor pleasure—this is called the illusion-like samādhi.
With this mouth born of my parents, I extend an immeasurable, broad, and long tongue, from which flows forth an ocean of all speech, manifesting the treasury of the Great Being’s merits.
The merits of the Great Being are boundless; likewise, these words of mine are inexhaustible, from dawn until dusk.
From month to year, they continue in succession without interruption; as it is in one place, so it is in all places.

Through seeing, hearing, and sympathetic joy, they mutually support one another, perfectly realizing the unsurpassed, wondrous Lotus Flower and abiding securely in the precious awakening of the Vajra King.
A lapis lazuli bowl filled with celestial ambrosia; boundless heat and affliction become a single flavor of cool clarity. Realizing true and perfect penetration, one attains great sovereignty.
Without moving from the fundamental limit, one universally responds to all diverse regions—like a steep, jagged cliff or an iron ridge suspended in mid-air.
The coiled branches extend outward, manifesting the vernal splendor beyond the kalpas. They reveal the wondrous realm of the Universal Gate and display the illusory Vajra.
As the brilliant sun adorns the heavens, nothing dark remains unilluminated; as the pure wind sweeps across the earth, its virtue is most clearly manifested.
The world of heaven and earth at the seashore stands solitary and absolute; white flowers intermingle with the fragrance of sandalwood.
Vastly drifting upon the ocean of fragrant waters, firmly perched upon the back of the golden tortoise. Having no volitional activity within the mind, one attains mastery over all phenomena.
The nectar of immortality within the flask; the realm of sentient beings before one’s eyes. This illusory samādhi cannot be destroyed even by being struck with an iron mallet.
With sincere devotion, a sudden resonance was felt; in dreams, wondrous lights and marvels appeared. It was like a magnet and a needle, where there is no obstruction at the point of union;
or like a great round mirror, where forms and reflections naturally merge. I am not separate from the Great Being (Mahāsattva), and the Great Being is not separate from me.
How magnificent is this Mountain of Merit! Facing every direction, it stands eternally before us (painted upon having experienced a dream).
Within the Great Perfect Illumination, the compassionate countenance of the Full Moon is revealed. The six sense faculties function interchangeably; the single nature is harmoniously integrated.

Layer upon layer, the waves of the Fragrant Water Sea rise; encircling the precious lotus throne, auspicious breezes swirl. Gathering all of the five turbidities back into pure tranquility, he utters the great lion’s roar.
Universally enlightening all who are deaf, this is what is called the Vajra Samādhi of hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation, which is like an illusion;
it does not move from the fundamental limit, yet reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions, being without coming or going, and complete in both beginning and end.

He opens the gate of universal penetration and preaches the Dharma of fearlessness. With eyes of compassion he gazes universally, and with a heart of compassion he gathers all beings. Within the tip of a single hair, the ten directions are revealed;
in a single kṣaṇa, ten thousand kalpas are encompassed. This is what is meant by donning the armor of diligence and generating a firm resolve:
to serve as a boat and as oars amidst the violent torrent of birth and death, neither retreating nor cowering.
Through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, one realizes the state of Avalokiteśvara and reveals the inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation.

Entering the Samādhi of Universal Delightful Vision, one proceeds directly forward; wondrously turning back from non-retrogression, the six sense-faculties function interchangeably—neither orthodox nor biased.
One contemplates the ocean of lands as a single field, without front or back.
The Dharma-gate is perfectly penetrating; samādhi is like an illusion. In a single thought-moment, one realizes all things, and they manifest universally throughout the ten directions.
Only this Great Being, through skillful means, gathers humans, devas, and nāgas and places them upon the shore of nirvāṇa. Seated, he cuts off the towering precipice of ten thousand fathoms;
while the earth rotates to the right, the heavens rotate to the left.
With his hair tied in two tufts at the temples, he bent his five fingers; having attained true *pariśuddhi* (perfect penetration), he universally bestows fearlessness.

The Dragon protects the Dharma and does not remain hidden; birds carry blossoms and arrive repeatedly. On the jade cliffs and gemstone trees, precious light floats; in the azure sea, there are no clouds, for the heavens are reflected in the water.
The Threefold Training in the Outflows-Free; how magnificent is the Universal Gate! With the faculty of hearing perfectly realized, one hears with the eyes.

One dries up the ocean of karma of all sentient beings and spreads the compassionate clouds of myriad virtues. Though the five aggregates are fundamentally empty, they are still used for illumination; though the body is covered in mud and water, how could it be divided?
Perfect penetration enters right contemplation; precipitous cliffs see flying waters fall. The great trichiliocosm is but a single hair-tip; the three periods of time are but a snap of the fingers.
The ocean of karma has no boundless shore—how could a compassionate heart not be moved? When both quiescence and illumination are forgotten, every thought arises from conditions.
The Vajra Samādhi, the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration: not hearing with the ears, but hearing with the eyes; entering the wisdom of all Buddhas and responding to the faculties of sentient beings.
Before the cliff, the suspended waterfall is three thousand *zhang* high; its vast sound and light pierce through the azure clouds.
The six faculties function with perfect penetration; a single mechanism is uniquely revealed. Face-to-face presentation leaves no room for evasion or detour.
What need is there to speak of the thirty-two transformations entering the bodies of various lands? To examine this thoroughly, it is simply like a scale-weight dipped in vinegar.
This Dharma is the essence of the true teaching; its purity resides in sound and hearing. How excellent is Avalokiteśvara, who has opened this wondrous gateway of the ear!
Steep cliffs and precipitous crags share a single tongue; jeweled clouds and incense seals fill the universe.

The gate of perfect penetration of the myriad dharmas: the reflection of a single moon in a thousand rivers. The essence of mind naturally transcends hearing; nature and characteristics are entirely equal.
Revealing half his body from a sheer cliff or a precipice, he sits loftily, severing all at the crown of Vairocana.

Sublime eloquence flows like a cascading torrent; meditative concentration is as steadfast as a mountain. The six faculties are universally perfected and penetrating; all sensory objects are luminously vast and clear.
From the beginning, the essence of sentient beings and Buddhas has been identical; even the white ox and the stray cat have attained perfect enlightenment.
Bubbles arise and bubbles perish; the torrent itself speaks the Dharma. The stone understands the essence of the Way.
The aspect of Great Compassion is quiescent yet ever-illuminating; even this illumination—what existence has it? The white sun shines brightly.

The Sea-Seal emits radiance; the jade pitcher is vast and empty. The moon fills the azure isles; the wind arises in the blue void. The Universal Gate manifests itself; its wondrous power is effortless.
It transcends the finest hair and the smallest speck; it is as stable as a mountain or a peak.
The white robes are not heavy; the lotus boat is naturally light. One perceives form within the ears and hears sound within the eyes. Once Sudhana departed, there has been no news.
When the winds of the ocean of awakening cease, the moon shines of its own accord.
He opens wide the gate of universal penetration and grasps the seal of Bodhi. With eyes and ears observing as one, wisdom and compassion operate in unison.
Silver mountains and iron walls reveal his total functioning; the boundless ocean of karma is emptied in a single instant.
Steep cliffs and hanging precipices; the springtime countenance and the moon’s reflection. Reaching the source of all dharmas, penetrating to the summit of the thousand sages.
A small white flower blooms before the great kalpa; amidst profuse activity, one eternally abides in the nāga-samādhi.

Correctly contemplating non-self, for whom do you extend your hand? The six sense organs function interchangeably; with equal compassion, they penetrate the Dharma-realm, empty across the three periods of time.
In every land and at every moment, they respond universally to the needs of the age.

Jewels are translucent; the jade pitcher is vast and empty. With a single root returning to the source, the six faculties cease their activity. The marks and signs of a child’s countenance are like a solitary moon-disk;
by the seashore, the wind is clear and the night tide has fallen.
The faculties and their objects share the same source; motion and stillness are non-dual. Ear and form, eye and sound—seeing and hearing transcend and reach the ultimate.
Standing alone before a precipice ten thousand fathoms high, the realm of the Universal Gate is neither heaven nor earth.

What moves? What is still? It is neither spring nor stone. What sees? What hears? It is neither sound nor form. The youthful one of true suchness bows his head, forgetting both words and the six faculties;
they are perfectly penetrating, spontaneously empty and quiescent.
The moon is in the sky; its reflection is contained within all waters. The practice of great compassion is simply this. To hesitate is like facing a precipice ten thousand fathoms high;
to lift one’s eyes is already three thousand miles away.
A single leaf of the lotus upon the boundless ocean of vows; the vast sky of the mind through the skillful means of the Universal Gate.
Without relying on the power of the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty perceives directly—this is the sovereign dhyāna of perfect penetration.

When one turns the hearing back toward itself, what is there after the hearing? When one turns the head back, there is no time when worldly toil has not yet ceased. Leaning alone against the azure cliff, I gaze at the flying waterfall;
the spring breeze does not reside in the green willow branches.
Rare are those who meet upon the realm of sentient beings; alone, one drifts slowly amidst the waves of the five desires.
Without self, without person, and without Buddha—how could this mind ever be known by Sudhana?
Upon the diamond-hard ground, the Water Deity opens the way; the youth comes from afar, seeking instruction in the South.
Within the eighty-four thousand oceans of affliction, where the waves crest high, there is but dust and grit.

The ocean of samādhi wherein the six sense-faculties function interchangeably; the body of Universal Joy to Behold (Sarvasattvapriyadarśana). A steady stream of spring water winds around the azure rocks;
upon the golden ground, not a speck of dust settles.

Sitting upright yet leaning back, looking down from above; through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, one enters samādhi. Spring returns to the steep cliffs where the *pi-li* and *chun* trees flourish;
the moon rolls across the vast ocean upon coral trees.
The golden scales within the basket have just shed their tides. Hearing the sound, he turns his head and enters the realm of worldly toil. It is simply because there is no market today;
do not say that the price the slave demands is high.
The body of skillful response is boundless and sovereign; clad in white robes with disheveled hair, it dwells not in dust. Such a way of life is difficult to accommodate;
it is only fitting to offer it to others with harmonious words.
Setting down the fish basket, he spreads out the sutra; the white lotus carries the scent of the scales of the brocade fish. The jade hook severs the crimson silk line;
the waters ripple over the golden sand as the moon fills the marsh.
Emerald cliffs and vermilion peaks; jade trees and crystalline herbs. The Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration shines like the bright, radiant sun.
Like flowers in the sky without stems, yet there is a vessel upon the ocean of vows. Leaning on his knee and looking down, he beholds the hundred rivers flowing toward their source.
Lapis lazuli gems; sandalwood-scented breezes; the practice of great compassion; the moon’s reflection and the springtime countenance;
the wondrous marks of a youthful sage; a compassionate face like the full moon; hearing back toward one's own nature; wind arising from suspended water.
The six faculties cease their activity and return to the source; this is the single, true, and perfect penetration. Amidst the azure cliffs and ancient trees, the spring wind blows beyond the kalpas.
This Dharma-gate of perfect penetration is profoundly empty of boundaries and limits; though the rocks split and the cliffs crumble, it reveals but a single aperture.
Hairpins askew and tresses disheveled; the mouth speaks one thing while the heart intends another. Failing to find a buyer for what she sells, she takes the fish back home.
Heard by the ears and seen by the eyes—among all phenomena, there is nothing to be grasped. Within the Great Perfect Illumination lies the Vajra Samādhi.
The six faculties are non-active; a single mechanism is revealed alone. The lion yawns; the elephant king looks back.

The Bagua Monk holds his golden staff upside down, resting securely upon his cloth bag. With brows lowered and eyes closed, shoulders bared and back exposed—he is still separated from Buddhahood by a hair’s breadth.
Throughout his life, he has entered the samādhi of drowsiness; even at the Dragon Flower Assembly, one could hardly find such freedom.
At the tip of his staff, there is both illumination and function; within his tattered cloth bag, there is no crack and no seam.
Having cast aside the Tuṣita Heaven, he loves to display his wares among men. I bow my head to the World-Honored One Maitreya: why are you so formal and grave?
Strange lights appear at the tips of his fingers as his true form manifests; though his belly is vast, his eyes have already grown dizzy.
He wanders recklessly through the homes of the noble clans, yet he cannot turn over a single cloth bag.
Hastening and hurrying, one runs through the market streets; meeting people, one stretches out a hand to beg for cash. On the tip of the staff, the sun and moon move within the light;
within the satchel, heaven and earth revolve in the dark.
The staff is long or short; the cloth bag is light or heavy. With a broad belly, he serves himself with a single laugh.
The Cloth Bag and the Fish Basket are depicted together in one scroll:
by the waterside of Changting, upon the sands of Jinsha—both possess a certain air of elegance, yet are ten times as reckless. Within this tattered cloth bag...
"Extremely precious pearls! A bottomless basket full of various fish. Carrying the entire burden upon one's shoulders. Meeting on a narrow path. Holding them bare-handed.
Never letting go while walking. Displaying such wonders to delude people—such a person deserves the staff held in my hand."

The two Great Beings, Hanshan and Shide, blended with worldly customs in their deportment yet maintained a transcendent bearing. What did they see? They laughed at themselves and clapped their own hands:
"The bright moon and clear wind comprise three hundred poems; though scattered throughout the human world, there is nowhere for them to settle."

Unfurling the sutra scrolls, looking left and right, up and down—the feet are thin while the shoes are wide; the hair is disheveled and the eyes spin. Among the myriad gates of practice, not a single dharma exists;
yet the divine mechanisms of hand and face undergo a thousand transformations every day.
Both eyes gaze at the ground; a single finger points to the heavens. It would be well to strike [the drum], yet one cannot advance.
The midday meal bell tolls at Guoqing Temple; a pity for the waterfall spring to the west of the cliff.
A single smile as the two brothers gaze at one another; their faces are covered in dust, their hair disheveled and wild.
A startling phrase that has no title—speak it for the myriad phenomena of the universe to hear.

The Arhat (6): Secretive within yet manifesting without; he flies over land and runs through the air. Dragons descend with fierce roars, tigers advance without a sudden bound, and monkeys present fruit before him.
The deer-flower followed behind; suddenly, he sat in the full lotus posture and turned like a king of elephants. His sneeze became a lion’s roar. "If it is deep, one wades through it;
if shallow, one steps over it"—such was his measured composure. The elderly carried the young, and the young led the way; there was nothing strange or unseemly about it.
