I smiled and said to them, "Is this something you people are capable of doing? As for the Dharma of a bhikṣu, one must internally subdue the conceit of self and externally sever all arrogance;
only then can one practice impartial compassion and spread a heart like the earth. Even then, one still fears..."
When encountering objects through sensory contact, there are circumstances that one simply cannot avoid;

how much more so for one who, from birth, has enjoyed complete autonomy, yet suddenly must humble oneself and submit to others—this is something rarely seen as acceptable. Nevertheless, Dongshan said: "Nothing is more humiliating than begging."
The ultimate joy lies in having no desires. If one truly attains the essence of desirelessness, even if one begs for food, what shame is there?
Vimalakīrti said: "He who is equal toward food is also equal toward the Dharma; he who is equal toward the Dharma is also equal toward food.
You may receive this food only if you can revile the Buddha, slander the Dharma, and cease to be counted among the ranks of the assembly. Go now, and take good care of yourself.

I have shown Master Cangzhu Fei that he has realized the mind and attained the fundamental source; for this reason, he is called a śramaṇa. This is not merely a matter of wearing square-cut robes and having a shaven head.
However, the substance of the mind is empty and tranquil, universally responding to myriad functions. Though it is active all day long, there are those who do not recognize it. To abandon it...
To seek elsewhere—seeking Buddhas and Patriarchs, seeking Chan and the Way—is truly a perversion.
If one awakens to one’s own mind and realizes its total, pervasive penetration, then one is neither bound by dharmas nor seeks liberation through them.

One will then see that the Buddhas, Patriarchs, Chan, and the Way are all complete within oneself, with not a single dharma arriving from without. Such a person is truly one who has settled the matter.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does even a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou replied, "No. This public case has circulated throughout the monastic community;
among those who study the Way, there are none who do not take it up for contemplation and investigation.
While many have indeed attained realization through it, there are also not a few who have misunderstood it. Master Wuzu said: "Zhaozhou revealed..."
A blade of sword, its cold frost shimmering with flame. If you further ask how it is so, your body will be divided into two pieces.
This is the very appearance of one who has seen where his tongue falls. Later, Master Fóxìng Tái said:
"With just this 'exposed blade of sword,' the whole matter has already been versified at once; the three subsequent lines are merely words of elaboration. How wondrous!

Xishi considered this to be so. He knew that one who has reached the bottom would bring it forth; thus, the singing and the clapping would naturally harmonize, and their words and spirit would accord.
As for those who rely on words and linger in phrases, or those who speculate with their conscious intellect—like those who press a map to seek a horse—they will be far from it for donkey-years.
The entire Tripitaka is merely a "cutting word" (a phonetic component). But tell me, what does it cut? Master Yanguan said:
"Po-ran-na. This old fellow first set out on his travels in his early years and met Master Fushan Yuanjian.
He once requested instruction on the story of Xinghua’s 'sudden wind and torrential rain. Yuanjian said, 'I have a parable for you:
a wood-seller from a village of three households has a shoulder pole laden with firewood, yet he asks the Hall of State Secretaries, "What is today's...'"
"What matter are you discussing? Zen Master Yuanwu then lowered his head and said, "If that is so, then it is still a great distance away.
Because he saw Baiyun bite through a single iron sour dumpling, all flavors were suddenly made complete; it was like a lion performing a backward somersault.
This was a startling moment. One day, Sanfoteli (Sengfu) stood up and asked, "The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories.
How would you explain this, Preceptor? The Patriarch replied, "It is like a mani jewel reflecting the five colors. The mani jewel is a metaphor for the Buddha-body.
The five colors are a metaphor for numbers. The three Buddhas withdrew and deliberated, saying, "This old fellow is truly a great beast!
If it were any of us, how could we have finished explaining this without using several sheets of paper?

Little did they realize that when a person of transcendent capacity addresses matters of transcendent scope, it naturally requires no effort. Have you not seen how, in the assembly of Vimalakīrti, each of the thirty-two bodhisattvas...

They preached the Dharma-gate of Non-duality, their words rising like clouds and pouring from flasks; none of them failed to claim that they had accorded with the principle and the capacity of the audience.

Yet Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word. Mañjuśrī then praised him, saying: "One should know that being without speech and without teaching is the true entry into the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.

*Du!* (A sharp exclamation) How well you recognize right and wrong! If one wishes to know the claws and fangs of the upward-pointing ancestral school, there are few who do not act in this manner. There is none.
He whose view is thoroughly liberated possesses sufficient power; naturally, the water reaches the ditch and the wind bends the grass, without ever expending effort.
Should his view not be thoroughly liberated and his power insufficient, he will rely on walls and lean against partitions, ultimately lacking any share of true freedom.
The entire great treasury of the teachings is, in essence, a medical manual for curing the madness of one’s own child.
If one penetrates to the fundamental source, the mad mind will suddenly cease, and one will naturally be able to let out a laugh. Nevertheless, such great kindness is difficult to repay.
Yongjia said: "When realized, karmic obstacles are originally empty; when not yet realized, one must repay past debts. How profound is this meaning!
The divine light is never obscured; it is a magnificent legacy for all eternity. Upon entering this gate, do not harbor intellectual understanding.

The intention of the ancients was never to have you sit in a state of soulless, certain death. You must know that those who fail to achieve realization mistakenly identify with the shadows of conceptual discrimination arising from sensory conditions.
Thus they lose their true nature and wander through the cycle of birth and death—all of which is the fault of intellectual understanding. If...

This transcends the emotions and leaves behind all views; it penetrates the fundamental source so that conceptual understanding no longer remains, yet there is nothing hidden that it does not illuminate.

It is like a person with clear vision, seeing without obstruction. As for those who feel like people groping for an elephant, though they compete with many divergent theories, they are all truly pitiable.

Attendant Shidou, the Great Way is right before your eyes; yet, for all its presence, it is difficult to behold. If you wish to recognize the true essence of the Great Way, it is not separate from sound, form, and speech.
Yet, when speech and activity are in motion, there is no point of contact at all. Ultimately, where does the true essence of the Great Way reside? It resides in Śrī.
Look at the ancient masters of old; they upheld this matter as the sun travels through the sky or the wind blows across the water.
A person of keen intelligence sees it upon a single glance, without relying on deliberation; yet the true essence of the Great Way does not admit even a hair’s breadth of separation.
This is what is meant: "A sudden snap, a sudden break—naturally so, without needing to breathe through another's nostrils.
When Buddhas and Patriarchs appear in the world, they do nothing more than provide for you a preliminary path; how could there be any dharma to be transmitted?
Therefore it is said: "The Great Matter cannot be taken over for you; each must take responsibility for it themselves. Ānanda said, "I had thought, World-Honored One..."
"Bestow upon me the samādhi. [The Master] said, "I do not know that body and mind fundamentally cannot substitute for one another;

is it not so? The Second Patriarch said, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to pacify my mind. Bodhidharma said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will pacify it for you. The Second Patriarch said:
When he sought his mind, it was utterly unattainable. Bodhidharma said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. This is truly like pushing a door into a mortar;
if one tries to fit a square hole with a round handle, there will never be a day when they correspond.
It is easy for a disciple to seek a teacher, but difficult for a teacher to find a disciple. Among the patriarchs of antiquity, they fished out but one or two from among tens of millions of people;
how is this different from sifting through sand to select gold? One should know that a true monk is truly not easy to find.
In the assembly at Huangmei, there were seven hundred followers, yet the robe and bowl were bestowed solely upon Layman Lu. How could this matter be...?

One may be coarse-minded; if one has not attained yet claims to have attained, or has not realized yet claims to have realized, and feels jealousy toward those who have made superior progress, such a person belongs to the class of those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

If you truly wish to investigate and clarify that single stroke upon the crown of the heads of the thousand sages, you must possess a body and mind of iron and stone, and have the spirit to swallow Buddhas and patriarchs; only then can you engage in this discourse. Have you not seen?
Among the more than seventy spiritual friends who participated in the Great Sui [assembly], those who possess the great eye of wisdom are but one or two.
Judging by this, it is not easy for a disciple to find a true teacher.
To Master Zong, the Abbot:

From Buddha to Buddha, hand has been passed to hand; from patriarch to patriarch, it has been transmitted from one to another. It is nothing other than the mind sealing the mind and the Dharma being entrusted to the Dharma.

Not even a single hair’s breadth has ever come from without. It is solely because of the convergence of like natures and the resonance of spiritual capacity that [the realization] can be brought forth.
Come! This naturally transcends the reach of ordinary thought. It is rooted in the True Cause (samyak-hetu) and remains untainted by deviant interpretations.
Like the Puṇḍarīka flower, though it grows from within the mud, not a single drop adheres to it. Yet its true nature is luminous and wondrous; it is inherently natural.
With a single thought of turning the light back upon itself, one is identical to all Buddhas. Have you not seen how when Damei saw Mazu, he simply—
Upon hearing the words "this very mind is Buddha," Bālananda immediately attained peace and bliss; when he was stepped upon by the water buffalo, he broke into a great laugh.
As for Xuefeng rolling the ball and Jushi raising his finger—these were all instances of revealing this unconditioned principle prior to the differentiation of sentient beings and Buddhas.
How could there be any secret transmission in a mysterious chamber that would lead to doubt and delusion for later generations?
Alas, students! In recent times, the Way of the Dharma has not flourished; erroneous interpretations abound, and each person claims to have attained the "Dharma of the Superior Man" (āryadharma).
They gather hundreds and thousands of followers, speaking in a jumble of foreign and Chinese tongues like those possessed by madness, utterly devoid of shame.

Yet they enter among their fellow practitioners; since their practice lacks the true cause, they have no blood beneath their skin and no sinews in their eyes. They imagine themselves to be Buddhas and patriarchs.

The Way has come to this; it is merely a matter of successive generations following one another, allowing the ancestral tradition to become overgrown and defiled—a state that truly merits great lamentation.

Unless one possesses innate spiritual bone from past lives, is not susceptible to deception, and is preeminent and transcendent enough not to be transformed along with the common flow, then in daily life and in responding to conditions, one must take the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity as one’s standard.
With single-minded devotion, one should give rise to great vows so that within this very life—
To accomplish matters of such great magnitude over hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, one must draw near to one or two true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Entering their crucible and receiving their tongs and hammers, one undergoes forging and polishing until all flaws and impurities are utterly severed; only then is it the time of arriving home.
Thereafter, one acts spontaneously in accordance with conditions, extending this realization to others to repay the Buddhas and Patriarchs, so that one’s efforts shall not be in vain.
He has come to the human realm to make one more turn.

He reveals to Attendant Yin the Treasury of the True Nature of the Mind-ground: it has neither head nor tail; responding to conditions, it transforms sentient beings, and for the sake of skillful means, it is called "wisdom."
How could one possibly attain it through the conceptualization of deliberate effort? One must simply sever all mental activity and discursive thought.
At all times, straighten your backbone and hold fast to a single kōan of the ancient masters with unwavering resolve.
Skillfully monitor your own state, keeping it sharp and alert so that you do not fall into the states of dullness or agitation; then, there will be vast, penetrating clarity.
Spiritual penetration is still, profound, and quiescent; one does not give rise to a second thought. Therefore it is said:
"Not setting oneself in opposition to all phenomena is itself the Samādhi of Non-contention. Yongjia said: "Neither person nor thing exists; the great chiliocosm is but a bubble in the sea.
All sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning. If one is coarse-minded, one might claim to have attained great peace and bliss.
This is precisely a great illness. The former sages identified it as a deep pit from which liberation is difficult. Those who still possess breath will never remain settled here.
Zhenjing said: "Vibrant and rolling, clear and falling; pick up and immediately rise, seize and immediately strike down.
Directly beneath, one is like a swift falcon or a rapid hawk—would such a one ever consent to kill a dead rabbit?"
Truth does not conceal falsehood; the crooked cannot hide the straight. With tiger-like strides and dragon-like gallops, gods cry out and ghosts weep. A man of clear vision has escaped the old nest;
he cuts through iron and chops through nails, shifting the stars and changing the constellations. A monk asked the National Teacher, "What is the Dharmakāya Vairocana?
The National Teacher said, "Hand me the pure water pitcher. The monk handed him the pitcher. The National Teacher said, "Return it."
He was settled in his former place, and the previous question was addressed again. The National Teacher said: "The ancient Buddhas passed away long ago.
Like sparks struck from flint or a flash of lightning—whether you grasp them or not, you cannot avoid losing your life.

How can this compare to those of today who take the 'donkey's head' or the 'horse's tail' as the ultimate principle? Having grasped a single thing, they immediately proceed to pierce it with intellectual analysis and provide commentaries."
To speak of "taking it away"—how could one know there is the matter of the Gate of the Patriarchs? But what, pray tell, is this matter of the Gate of the Patriarchs?
*Duh!* Only the Old Barbarian is permitted to know; the Old Barbarian is not permitted to understand.

Before the sound reaches the ear, one may grasp the essential meaning, yet remain confused regarding the source of the reflection; after the phrase is uttered, one may clarify the fundamental principle, yet still be ignorant of what lies beyond the realm of conceptual consciousness.
A single thought tied to even a hair’s breadth is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting stir of emotion results in shackles for ten thousand kalpas.
One must be like the Lion King, letting out a single roar that causes all foxes and jackals to vanish from sight; only then can one act as the true foundation.

The Way has split into factions. If one merely follows the crowds and keeps company, with intoxicated countenance and heavy voice, indulging in nothing but reckless madness to deceive gods and frighten ghosts;

if, wherever one meets people, one flaunts a muddled bag of talk, claiming "I can" and "I understand," thereby ruining the fine sayings of the ancients, and furthermore teaches others to deceive one another and trample upon the ancestral style—this is truly a disaster for the earth.
The prison is the seed. You, the younger generation, while your physical strength and vigor are yet robust, must swiftly resolve upon the clarity of the teachings.
Upon seeing such people as these, you ought to treat them with reverence from a distance; there is truly no need to contend with them over gain or loss.
Simply reflect that since immeasurable kalpas past, you have been submerged and emerged within the ocean of birth and death; now, by good fortune, you have become human and encountered [the Dharma].

Regarding the Holy Teachings: having donned the dharma robes and roughly assumed the title of śramaṇa, let us examine the Elder Śākyamuni—his birth from the womb, his cultivation of the Way, his attainment of Buddhahood, and his saving of sentient beings—from where did all these dharma-gates originate?

Furthermore, after his parinirvāṇa, as the Great Dharma gradually spread to the East and successive patriarchs arose to uphold the seal of orthodoxy, they displayed a truly remarkable character. It is just as it was said: "The Way has not yet left Tuṣita..."
He had already descended into the royal palace, yet not yet emerged from his mother’s womb; his work of saving sentient beings was already complete.
Furthermore, it is said that from the Deer Park until the end at the Bahudā River, in the interval between these two, he never spoke a single word.

Moreover, throughout forty-nine years and over three hundred assemblies, with their various modes of conduct—how can these be accounted for? When one arrives here, if even a single dharma is not understood, it is a cataract.
O you, whose eyesight is dim, the world appears treacherous and vast. Should you suddenly fail to draw another breath, you will immediately ascend to the registers of the hungry ghosts.

The path ahead is long and endless; one knows not where it leads. This is truly a matter for heart-rending grief. Therefore, the former masters held that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence is swift, keeping this deeply in their hearts.
As long as the Great Matter is not clarified, they feel as if they have lost both parents; once the Great Matter is realized, [they are at peace].
To be enlightened is like mourning for one’s deceased parents; how could there be leisure for idle sentiments? How could one find peace in trivial matters?

To Master Xing, I show that within the School of the Patriarchs, we value only true inquiry and actual realization. It requires nothing more than a single cry of "Agh! to naturally penetrate to the very summit.
To the very bottom. If you have not attained this understanding, your mind will inevitably remain stifled and oppressed, unable to find joy.
It is like a person suffering from illness who has been struck by wind and cold;
suddenly obtaining a potent medicine, they break into a profuse sweat and realize how much relief there is for the four great elements. Once that relief is attained, one must nevertheless...

Nourish your spirit and restore its equilibrium; only then can you maintain the restraint against stumbling. Should you fail to guard it even once, and your old afflictions recur, then there will be no way to save you.

Were one to involve discursive thought, however, white clouds would stretch for ten thousand miles.
Simply attain the root and do not worry about the branches. What is called the root? What is called the branches? Recognizing the mind and seeing one's nature is the root;

discoursing on Chan and speaking of the Way are the branches. If you have recognized the mind and seen your nature, then whatever you speak from the heart of faith and whatever you walk with the feet of faith is none other than Chan and the Way.
If you neglect the root while grasping at the branches, this is what is meant by "karmic consciousness wandering aimlessly, with no root to rely upon."

Accordingly, those who study the Way do not recognize the Real because they have been identifying with the spirit since time immemorial. This is the root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas;
yet deluded people call it the "original person. Students who are not skilled at making distinctions falsely identify with the cognizing mind and take it to be [the self].
Regarding oneself, as it is said in the teachings: "To mistake a thief for one's own son, one will never succeed in securing the family’s wealth and treasures.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Dharma is free from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. If one acts through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, this is merely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing;
it is not the seeking of the Dharma. The Great Master Huineng said: "Hearing, seeing, sensing, and knowing are without obstruction; sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena are ever..."
Samādhi. Like a bird flying through the air, there is neither grasping nor rejecting, neither aversion nor attachment.
This is the talk of one who has finally arrived home. To achieve resonance, before even a single thought has arisen, look with urgent eyes. *Du!* (A sharp exclamation).

In studying this Way, what is valued is treading upon solid ground and acting with reliance on reality. If there is even a hair’s breadth of grasping at the void, one falls entirely into the realm of Māra.
Regarding the first step, let us discuss having a clear realization of the Ground (dṛṣṭi-bhūmi) so that one is not deluded by external conditions;

in this way, you will gain power throughout the twelve periods of the day. If your vision is not thoroughly liberated, how can you accomplish matters that transcend ordinary limits? Thus spoke the Ancients.
Regarding the Way of Virtue: even if there were a single dharma that surpassed nirvana, I would say it is likewise like a dream or an illusion.
If one’s own eye has not yet opened, how can one understand this? This is the place where those of the highest rank tread;
it is like a vajra-flame, like a mass of fierce fire—there is no way for you to draw near. It is not that I am being forceful; such is the nature of the Dharma.
The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally without mystery or subtlety; it is simply one’s own original portion of reality.

It is only because people have abandoned their home and lost their occupation, wandering for a long time, that upon first entering the gate, they find it strange and marvelous. Once they sit securely within the hall of their own house, all phenomena are nothing but the ordinary;
naturally, there is no cause for alarm or wonder. Linji said: "It turns out that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma..."
There are not many [who attain it]. This is precisely the news. The Way of the Buddha is vast and remote;
only after enduring diligent suffering for a long time can one achieve its fulfillment. It is not a matter of merely seeing it and understanding it and then stopping there.
Those former sages entered the water and entered the mud, dwelling securely in the realm of great beings where there is no effortful application (*anābhoga*). How could it be otherwise?
How coarse of mind! Monks of the末法 (mofa) age obtain a mere fragment of influence and immediately claim that everything is settled and all matters resolved.
They do not read the sutras nor pay homage to the Buddha; they are uniformly arrogant and falsely exalt themselves, seeking the praise of others to secure gain and offerings.
They deceive one another, and this has become a habitual custom—truly pitiable. Those with resolve must, indeed, [apply themselves].
The ancients established these as guiding standards; be careful not to follow them in a perverted way.

This instruction to the Lamp Repository Master (Deng Cangzhu) from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity shows that there is no better way to cause each person to realize their own original mind and original nature than this. Do not...
Being enticed by external objects is merely a matter pertaining to the mundane world; it does not mean that there is some separate dharma to be transmitted or bestowed.
Rather, throughout the twelve periods of daily life, one must apply oneself with intense vigor and brilliance, maintaining a state of empty luminosity and tranquil illumination.

One should sever all conditions and remain detached and non-active, yet without hindering the free response to circumstances. When the practice becomes mature and integrated into a single whole, one may proceed as one pleases.
One acts by means of one's own power. Whenever there is even a slight matter that benefits others, one performs it with courage;

as for matters that bring no benefit, one does not engage in them again, nor does one harbor any notion of agency regarding what is done or not done, remaining utterly detached from all marks of achievement.
When meritorious achievements cease, the thoughts of gain and loss no longer arise. Yet, within the realms of adversity and favor, one does not cling to them but clearly realizes them;
thus, they are quiescent in their very essence. As the Patriarch said: "The mind turns with the myriad objects; where it turns, there is profound stillness.

If you recognize your nature while following the flow, there is neither joy nor sorrow. This is what is meant by "a single state of equanimity, wherein all things naturally vanish into extinction."—The Ancient Sage.
The proclamation of even a single word or half-phrase is entirely for the sake of compassion.

It is to manifest that one pivotal point where the thousand sages could not turn their eyes, in order to shatter the emotional attachments of future generations. The aim is to become a person who is free, unencumbered, and open;
how could there be any subtle mystery worth concealing or cherishing? Later generations, being mediocre and reckless, lacking any fundamental knowledge, took...

Each claims for themselves the attainment of the dharmas of a superior person, deceiving one another and misleading both themselves and others—a state truly worthy of deep sighs. This can only be remedied by past... [karmic roots].

Otherwise, if there are merely empty words without the corresponding resolve, then as the saying goes: "Though the body has left the household life..."
If the mind does not enter the Way, it will ultimately be captured by false teachers; of this there is no doubt. An ancient said: "To reach heights, one must rely on hills and mounds;
to reach depths, one must rely on rivers and marshes. For those in the lineage of the patched-robed monks, every movement and every stillness—should they not be cautious?
To the Head Seat Jue, he showed that the stream of Caoxi is not still water; when a single drop suddenly arrives, a thousand waves compete to rise. It is clearly the case that this principle exists.

You must know that the matters above the level of the Gate of the Patriarchs are categorically distinct. Even if you have ultimately reached a ground free from doubt, if the Great Dharma is not clear, it will all amount to nothing more than chaff.

"Go! Get out! Daie heard this and said, "How could the winds of karma have blown you all the way to the gate of Daie?

The next day, as Hua was passing by the Dharma Hall, Jue called to the head attendant, saying, "I have no doubt at all about your two shouts yesterday.
Explain them to me; one who acts for others must act with urgency. Hua replied, "I, your servant, regarding..."
"The three sages each attained a phrase regarding host and guest; they have all been defeated by my elder brother. Give me a Dharma-door of peace and ease.
[The Master replied: "A rat entering an ox's horn. Jue said, "You blind fellow! You come here to suffer defeat!
He stripped off his patched robe and struck him a severe blow. "To kill a man, one must see blood. [Jue] was transformed beneath the staff and came to understand.
Linji’s experience of receiving blows at Huangbo’s place was like refined gold tempered a hundred times;
it required the authentic tongs and hammer. How could it be a livelihood wrapped in hemp and paper?
This account has remained within my breast for many years, and I have never dared to casually bring it forth to others. My Dharma nephew, the Head Seat Benxin Jue, from Cao... [text continues]
Master Xifen arrives; the true eye at the crown of his head pierces through the four worlds. Yuchuang has brought it forth to nourish the joy of the Dharma.
Tomorrow I shall return to the East and see Old Master Songyue; I trouble you to inquire for me: where is this news to be found now?
It would be no small matter if you would convey it to me by way of the wind. I would be most grateful.

The Abbot Zhichang demonstrates that on the ground of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), not a single speck of dust is received; yet when principle follows the transformations of phenomena, not a single dharma is abandoned within the gateway of the myriad practices.

When phenomena attain harmony with principle, phenomena and principle are fused. This vast expanse is not external; this is principle following the transformations of phenomena. It is silent and desolate.

It is not internal. Since ancient times, when the realized masters have reached the point where the sentiments of both the holy and the ordinary are exhausted, their true permanence is naturally revealed.

Encountering things and responding to conditions, they meet everything before their eyes without obstruction; yet even this is not the place where those of the highest path tread. Therefore, the Great Master Yunmen said:
"Even if you could reach the point where the entire universe and the great earth are free from the slightest flaw or affliction, it is still a 'turning phrase. You do not see [the ultimate]."
"A single color" is merely half of the teaching; one must further know the occasion for the full presentation.

Some people, having recognized a mere shadow or reflection, immediately claim to be Yangs or Zhengs, looking down upon the four seas with empty eyes and misleading future students—this is shedding the blood of the Buddha.
If one has the "tendon in the eye," one will never allow oneself to be caged by such talk; they take a step and sweep it all away.
